en: Now begins the fourth chapter.
[In this chapter on the fruits [of yoga], the first section (pāda) treats the definition of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
1. The Section on Repetition (āvṛtty-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 1–2.
There is repetition because of repeated instruction.
In the third chapter, the investigation concerning the means based on the higher and lower knowledges has for the most part been completed;
now, in this fourth chapter, that which concerns the results will follow.
In this context, some other matters will also be considered as they arise.
First, however, we shall follow up on the remainder of our investigation into the locus of the means of proof (*sādhana*) through several topics.
"Indeed, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6).

Regarding such scriptural passages as "The wise man, having known that very [Self], should practice wisdom" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6) and "That is to be sought, that is to be desired to be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1), a doubt arises: should the realization be performed only once, or should it be repeated?
What, then, is the prima facie position? It should be that the cognition occurs only once, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth;
for by that much, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled.
If it were performed when [the time] is not being heard [prescribed], it would result in acting contrary to the meaning of the scripture.
But surely, repeated instructions have been cited, such as "it is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon," and so forth.
Even so, one should repeat [the practice] only as far as the word [of the scripture] indicates—once for hearing, once for reflection, and once for meditation—and nothing more than that.
However, in cases where the instruction is given only once, such as "one should worship" (*upāsīta*) and the like, there is no repetition.
This being the case, we reply: the repetition of the cognitive process must be performed.
Why? Because of the repeated instruction.
For such repeated instructions as "it is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" indicate the necessity of repeating the cognitive process.
But was it not said that one should repeat only as much as the word [prescribes] and no more? No;
there is no fault, because it culminates in direct perception (*darśana*).
For hearing and the other stages, when repeated until they culminate in direct perception, have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).
Just as threshing and other such processes culminate in the production of rice and the like, so it is in this case.
Moreover, both *upāsana* (worship) and *nididhyāsana* (meditative reflection) denote an action whose essential quality is the attribute of repetition (*āvṛtti*).
For instance, in common usage, one who follows a teacher or a king with total devotion is said to "worship" (*upāste*) them;
likewise, a woman whose husband is away who remembers him incessantly out of longing is said to "meditate" (*dhyāyati*) upon her husband.
Furthermore, in the Vedāntas, the terms *vid* (to know) and *upāsti* (to meditate upon) are seen to be used interchangeably;

in some places, having begun with *vid*, it concludes with *upāsti*, as for example: "He who knows what he knows—of that I have spoken to you" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.4), and here [the teacher says], "Sir, instruct me further regarding that deity whom you meditate upon" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.2).

And in some cases, having begun with "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*), he concludes with "one who knows thus," as for example: "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.1), and here [he concludes]:
"He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.3).
Therefore, even when the instruction is given only once, the accomplishment of repetition is established.
The repeated instruction, however, indicates the necessity of repetition. // 1 //
And from an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

An indicative mark also makes known the repetition of the meditative realization (*pratyayāvṛtti*); for instance, having introduced the knowledge of the *udgītha*, [the text says] "The sun is the *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.5.1).

Thus, having set aside the defect of having only one son, the text— "He should turn back the rays"— (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.5.2), by enjoining the knowledge of the multiplicity of rays for the sake of having many sons, shows the repetition of the meditative realization as an established fact.
Therefore, by analogy with that, the necessity of repetition is established for all forms of meditative realization.

To this, it is said: Let it be granted that there is repetition (*āvṛtti*) in the case of cognitions whose fruits are yet to be accomplished, because in those cases the possibility of an excellence produced by repetition exists.

But as for the cognition whose object is the Supreme Brahman—which presents the Supreme Brahman as one's own self, characterized by the nature of being eternally pure, conscious, and free—what is the purpose of repetition there?

If it is argued that repetition must be admitted because the realization of Brahman as the Self is impossible upon hearing [the teaching] only once, we say no; for even with repetition, that realization remains impossible.
For if [it were otherwise], regarding "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7):

If a statement of this kind, when heard only once, were unable to produce the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self, what hope could there be that the very same statement, when repeated, will produce it? Now,

if it should be argued that a sentence alone cannot effect a direct realization of any object, and therefore the sentence, depending upon reasoning (*yukti*), will cause one to experience the identity of Brahman and the Self— even so, repetition remains utterly useless.
For that reasoning, too, once set in motion, will indeed cause its own object to be experienced.
Furthermore, it might be argued that through speech and verbal expression, a cognition is produced only with respect to a general object, not a particular one.

For example, from the statement "I have a pain in my heart," or from signs such as trembling of the limbs, another person perceives only the general existence of the pain, but does not experience its particularity, just as [the patient himself does].

If it is argued that the Self is indeed possessed of attributes (*śūlin*), and that specific experience (*viśeṣānubhava*) is what removes ignorance, and therefore repetition is for that purpose— this is not so;
because even if one were to perform [the meditation] only that much repeatedly, the arising of specific cognition (*viśeṣavijñāna*) would still be impossible.
For a distinction that is not apprehended by scripture (*śāstra*) and reasoning (*yukti*) when they are applied once cannot be apprehended even if they are applied a hundred times.

Therefore, whether a distinction is established by scripture and reasoning, or only a generality, in either case, those two perform their own function as soon as they have operated once; thus, repetition (*āvṛtti*) is useless.
Nor can it be maintained that scripture and reasoning, when applied once, do not produce an experience for anyone, because of the diversity of the intelligence of those who understand.

Moreover, in the case of worldly objects which possess multiple parts and consist of both general and particular aspects, it may be that one perceives one part with one act of attention and another part with another, such that practice is useful— as in the case of learning long recitations and the like.

But in the case of Brahman, which is devoid of distinctions, free from general and particular aspects, and consists solely of pure consciousness, it is not logical to require practice for the arising of valid knowledge.

To this it is replied: Repetition would be purposeless for one who is able to realize the identity of Brahman and the self (*brahmātmatva*) immediately upon the statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) being uttered once;
however, for one who is not so able, repetition is indeed useful.
For instance, in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "That thou art, Śvetaketu" (Chā. 6.8.7).
Having thus instructed him with the words, "May the Blessed One inform me further," and being urged again, he dispels each respective cause for doubt and repeatedly teaches, "That thou art."
And thus it has been shown in such passages as, "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6).

Now, an objection is raised: if the statement "That thou art," when heard but once, is unable to bring about the experience of its own meaning, then even if it is repeated, it will certainly not be able to do so.
This is not a fault;
for indeed, there is nothing that is impossible regarding what is observed.

For we see those who, having understood the meaning of a sentence only dimly from hearing it once, repeat it while setting aside various fallacious appearances, thereby attaining the correct understanding.

Moreover, this sentence "That thou art" teaches that the referent of the word *tvam* (thou) has the nature of the referent of the word *tat* (that). By the word *tat*, the previously mentioned Being (*sat*), Brahman—the seer and the cause of the origin and so forth of the world—is denoted, as in: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1) and "Brahman is Consciousness and Bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28).
"The unseen seer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11);
"the unknown knower" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11);
"unborn, undecaying, immortal, neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8).
This and more is well known from the scriptures.
In that context, by words such as "unborn" (*aja*), the modifications of being such as birth and so forth are excluded;
and by words such as "not gross" (*asthūla*), the attributes of substance such as grossness and so forth are excluded.

Furthermore, by terms such as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and so forth, its nature as the light of pure sentience is expressed. This entity, which is devoid of all the attributes of transmigratory existence, whose essence is experience, and which is designated as Brahman, is well-known among those proficient in the Vedānta as the referent of that term.
Likewise, the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (you), which is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as the listener, is conceived as being within the body and determined to extend up to pure consciousness.

In this regard, for those whose knowledge of these two referents is obstructed by ignorance, doubt, or misconception, the sentence "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) is unable to produce valid cognition regarding its own meaning, because the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the knowledge of the meanings of its constituent words.

Thus, for this reason, one must apply oneself to the practice of the study of the scriptures and reasoning, which has as its purpose the discernment of the categories of existence (*padārtha-viveka*). And although the Self to be realized is partless (*niraṃśa*), nevertheless, many parts characterized by the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, and sensations have been superimposed upon it; therein, by means of a single point of concentration, one [should grasp] one part.
It is logical that there is a sequential realization in the sense that "one [cognition] removes another";
however, that [sequential process] is merely the prior form of the realization of the self.
But for those of subtle intellect, there is no obstruction regarding the objects of things characterized by ignorance, doubt, or error.
If it is possible for them to experience the meaning of the statement "That thou art" upon being told just once, then the futility of repetition is indeed accepted.
For the realization of the Self, having arisen just once, removes ignorance; thus, no sequence whatsoever is admitted here.
This would indeed be correct if anyone were to have such a realization;
for the realization of one's own suffering and so forth is powerful.
Therefore, if it is argued that no one realizes the non-existence of suffering and so forth, we say: no.
For the conceit of being a sufferer and so forth is established as a false conceit, just like the conceit [of being the body] regarding the body and such.
Indeed, it is observed that when the body is being cut or burned, there is a false conceit: "I am being cut," "I am being burned.
Likewise, even with respect to external things such as sons and friends, when they are suffering, an imposition is observed such as, "I myself am suffering," and so on.
Likewise, there would also be the conceit of being a sufferer and so forth;
for, like the body and other such things, suffering and its like are perceived as external to consciousness, and they do not persist during states such as deep sleep.

Indeed, they declare that consciousness persists even in deep sleep, through such passages as: "Verily, when there he does not see, he is indeed seeing, though he does not see" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).
Therefore, this experience of the Self is "I am," consisting of pure consciousness and entirely liberated from all suffering.
For one who experiences the Self in this way, no further duty remains.
Thus says the Śruti: "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Thus, [the author] shows the absence of anything to be done for one who knows the Self.
Smṛti also says: "But for that person who rejoices only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who finds contentment in the Self alone, no duty remains" (Gītā 3.17).
However, for one in whom this realization does not arise immediately, repetition is accepted for the sake of that very realization.
Even in that case, one should not engage them in repetition by diverting them from the meaning of the sentence "That thou art";
for they do not marry off a bride in order to kill the groom.

Furthermore, for one who has been appointed to this [task], the thought arises: "I am authorized; I am the agent; this was done poorly by me due to lack of intelligence. From that conviction regarding Brahman (*brahmapratyaya*), a contrary conviction arises.

However, for one who is himself dull-witted and, due to lack of intelligence, wishes to abandon that meaning of the sentence, the stabilization of that very meaning of the sentence through repetition and so forth is accepted as a logical method of instruction.
Therefore, even regarding the conviction concerning the Supreme Brahman, the necessity of repetition is established in the instructions on its means. // 2 //
2. The Section on the Meditation on the Self (Ātmatva-upāsanā-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 3:
"But they approach [the Self] as the 'Self' and cause [others] to grasp it as such.
(BBs 4.1.3) This section examines whether that Supreme Self, characterized by the attributes mentioned in the scriptures, is to be grasped as "I" or as "other than me."
But how can there be doubt when the word "Self" (ātman), which refers to the inner self, is being heard?

It is said in reply: This word "Self" can be accepted as primary if the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is possible; otherwise, however, one might think that this must be accepted as secondary. What, then, is the initial position? That it should not be grasped as "I."

For qualities such as being free from evil cannot be apprehended as having contrary qualities, nor can that which has contrary qualities be apprehended as having qualities such as being free from evil.
Furthermore, the Supreme Lord possesses qualities such as being free from evil, whereas the embodied soul (śārīra) possesses qualities contrary to those.
If the Lord were identical with the transmigrating soul, it would follow that the Lord does not exist.
Consequently, the scripture would be rendered purposeless.
Even if transmigrating beings were identical in nature with the Lord, the scripture would still be purposeless due to the absence of any qualified recipient for its teachings,
and there would also be a contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition.
If it is argued that even when there is difference, one must perceive identity based on scripture—just as one perceives Viṣṇu and others in images and the like—we grant that this may be so;
however, we are not led to the conclusion that the Lord is the primary Self of the transmigrating soul.
This being the position, we reply: the Supreme Lord is to be understood as the Self alone.

For instance, in the *Parameśvara-prakriyā*, the Jābālas approach this very [Self] as the Self itself, saying: "O Venerable One, I am indeed You, the Divine; You, O Venerable One, are indeed I, the Divine.
Likewise, other approaches to the Self, such as "I am Brahman," and so forth, are to be understood in the same way.
Moreover, the Vedānta texts cause one to grasp Īśvara as the very Self, as in: "This is your Self that is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1);
"This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3);
and "That is the Truth, That is the Self; Thou art That" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
Such [passages] as these [are cited].

As for the claim that this "vision of the prototype" (pratīkadarśana) will occur according to the principle of the Viṣṇu-image, that is incorrect, because it would entail a figurative sense (gauṇatva) and because of the disparity between the statements.

For where a perception of a symbol (*pratīka*) is intended, the statement is made only once, as in "The mind is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.1) or "The sun is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1), and so forth.
But here, on the other hand, he says: "I am thou, and thou art I."
Therefore, because of the dissimilarity in the scriptural mention of the *pratīka* (symbolic representation), there is no realization of non-difference;
furthermore, this is because of the censure of the perception of difference.
For it is said: "Now, he who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
"From death to death he goes who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19)— such abundant scriptural passages as these refute the perception of difference.
As for what was said— that two things with contradictory qualities cannot arise from one another's self— [that is not so].
This is not a fault,
because falsity is established through the presence of contradictory qualities.
As for what was further stated— that it would follow that God does not exist— [that too is not a fault].
That is incorrect, because it contradicts the authority of the scripture and because we do not accept that position.

For we do not maintain that the Lord's nature as a transmigrating being is being taught; rather, what is intended to be established is that the transmigrating being’s nature as the Lord is to be realized through the removal of its state as a transmigrator.

This being the case, it is established that in non-duality, the Lord possesses qualities such as being free from sin and so forth, whereas the contrary qualities belong to the other [the individual soul] and are therefore illusory.
As for what was also stated— that there is an absence of qualified candidates and a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge—
that too is incorrect.
Because transmigratory existence is admitted prior to awakening, and because empirical transactions such as perception and so forth have that [transmigratory state] as their object;
for it is said: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).
For by such statements as these, he demonstrates the non-existence of perception and the other means of knowledge upon awakening.
If it is argued that, in the absence of perception and the rest, there would follow the non-existence of scripture (*śruti*) as well, we say no; for this is precisely what is intended.

Having begun with the statement, "In this state, the father becomes no father" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.22), the text continues with the words, "The Vedas become non-Vedas" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.22);
therefore, we indeed accept that even the Śruti ceases to exist upon awakening.
If it is asked, "Whose is this lack of awakening?
we reply: "It belongs to you, whom you yourself are asking about.
But surely, it has been stated by the Śruti that you are indeed Īśvara?
If you have awakened in this way, there is no one left in a state of non-awakening.
Furthermore, the objection raised by some—that because ignorance (avidyā) would be a second entity to the Self, non-duality (advaita) would be untenable—is also refuted by this very point.
Therefore, one should fix the mind on the Lord as being simply the Self. // 3 //
3. The Section on the Symbol (Pratīka-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 4:
"Not in the symbol, for he [is not there].
Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.1 states: "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman—this with reference to the self; now with reference to the divine, one should meditate on space as Brahman."

In regard to meditations on symbols such as "The sun is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1) and "He who meditates on Name as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.5), a doubt arises: should the grasping of the Self be performed in these cases as well, or not?
What, then, is the conclusion?
Even in those cases, it is logical that there is precisely the grasping of a self.
Why?

"Because Brahman is well-known in the Śrutis as the Self, and because the symbols (pratīkas) are also modifications of Brahman, it is logical that they possess the nature of the Self while being Brahman. This being the position reached, we reply: one should not fix the notion of the Self upon the symbols. For that worshiper should not conceive of the symbols as separate things as being the Self.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the symbols (pratīkas) possess the nature of Brahman because they are modifications of Brahman, and consequently possess the nature of the Self—
that is incorrect;
for it would entail the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of the symbols themselves.
For when the nature of the modification is sublated, the name and so forth, being born, come to rest in Brahman-ness alone.
And when their own nature is sublated, how could there be the status of a symbol (*pratīka*) for the name and so forth, or the grasping of them as the Self?
Nor, because Brahman is the Self, should the view of the Self be inferred in those teachings that enjoin the contemplation of Brahman.
Because agency and so forth are not negated;
for it is only when agency and other such qualities of transmigratory existence have been negated that there is the teaching of Brahman as the Self,
whereas the injunction for meditation is established by not negating them.
And for this reason, because the worshipper is identical with the symbols (*pratīka*), the grasping of them as the Self (*ātmagraha*) is not tenable;
for there is no mutual identity between a necklace and a svastika.
We have already stated that if they were one through the nature of Brahman—as they are one through the nature of gold—then it would follow that the symbols would cease to exist.
Therefore, the view of the self is not to be applied to the symbols. // 4 //
4. The Section on the Vision of Brahman (Brahmadṛṣṭy-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 5:
"The vision of Brahman [is to be superimposed], because of superiority.

Regarding those very examples, another doubt arises: should the visions of the sun and so forth be superimposed upon Brahman, or should the vision of Brahman be superimposed upon the sun and so forth?
Whence arises this doubt? Because the cause for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not determined.

For here, the word "Brahman" is observed to be used in grammatical coreferentiality with words such as "Āditya," as seen in expressions like "The Sun is Brahman, the Breath is Brahman, Lightning is Brahman," due to the indication of identical case endings.
Moreover, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not directly possible here,
because the words "Brahman," "Āditya," and so forth, denote different objects;
for coreferentiality does not exist between [the terms] "cow" and "horse."

Objection: Since there is a relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of Brahman with the suns would be like that of clay with a bowl and so forth.
Reply: This is not so;
for if it were thus, there would be a dissolution of the modifications (*vikāra-pravilaya*) due to their coreferentiality with the material cause.
Furthermore, we have already stated that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of the absence of specific meditative images (*pratīka*).
Moreover, in that case, this would become a statement concerning the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), whereby the qualification for meditation (*upāsanā*) would be sublated,
and the recourse to a limited modification (*vikāra*) as a substrate would be rendered useless.

Therefore, just as in the case of "The Brāhmaṇa is Agni Vaiśvānara" and so forth, when there is an imposition (*adhyāsa*) consisting of the perception of one thing upon another, a doubt arises as to where and what perception should be imposed. In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no restriction, because there is no scriptural authority (*śāstra*) to impose such a restriction.
Alternatively, the prima facie view is that the perceptions of the sun and so forth should indeed be applied to Brahman.
For it is the established rule of the scriptures that Brahman is worshipped through such visions as those of the sun and so forth, and that the worship of Brahman is fruitful;
therefore, the vision of Brahman does not apply to the sun and other such objects.
This being the position reached, we reply: the vision of Brahman alone should indeed be applied to the sun and the rest.
Why?
Because of their excellence;
for it is through such excellence that the sun and other celestial bodies are perceived.
This is because of the superimposition of the perception of the superior upon them;
and thus the worldly maxim is followed.
For it is a worldly maxim that the perception of the superior is to be superimposed upon the inferior.
Just as the king's gaze is directed toward the attendant,
so too must he be followed;
for in the contrary case, there would be the consequence of transgression.
For a king who is embraced by the perspective of a charioteer would not lead to his own welfare when being led into degradation.

[Objection: Surely, on account of the authority of the scriptures (*śāstra*), the possibility of sin (*pratyavāya*) here is not to be suspected; moreover, it is not proper to restrict a scriptural perspective by means of worldly logic.
To this it is replied: This would indeed be so, provided that the meaning of the scripture were already definitively determined.
When there is doubt regarding that [matter], even a worldly principle (*nyāya*) being resorted to for the sake of a definitive conclusion is not contradictory.
Therefore, it follows that if one were to superimpose a lower vision while determining the meaning of the scripture through the superimposition of a higher vision, one would incur sin.
Furthermore, because they appear first and because there is no contradiction, the primary meaning of the words "Āditya" and so forth must be accepted.

Since the word *brahman* cannot enter into grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the primary sense when the intellect has already been occupied by those [words] functioning for their own specific referents, it must remain solely for the purpose of enjoining the contemplation (*dṛṣṭi*) of Brahman upon them;
moreover, because the word *brahman* functions as "thus" (*iti*), this very meaning is the most logical.

For instance, in all such passages as "Brahman is the instruction," "One should meditate on [it] as Brahman," and "One meditates on [it] as Brahman," the word *brahman* is uttered followed by the particle *iti*, whereas the words *āditya* and so forth are used in their pure, literal sense.

Consequently, just as in the expression "one perceives mother-of-pearl as silver," the word *śuktikā* (mother-of-pearl) denotes the actual object, while the word *rajata* (silver) is used figuratively to indicate the cognition of silver;
for one merely perceives "silver," yet no silver actually exists there.
Thus, it is understood that here too one should perceive Āditya and the others as Brahman;

for the remainder of the passage also shows, by means of the accusative case, that it is Āditya and the others who are pervaded by the act of meditation: "He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon Āditya as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.4), and "He who meditates upon speech as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.2.2).
And [it says], "He who meditates on volition as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.4.3).
As for what was said— that here meditation on Brahman alone is to be emphasized for the sake of the fruit—
that is incorrect.
According to the reasoning already stated, it is understood that only Āditya and the others are the objects of worship.

As for the fruit, however, just as in the case of worshipping guests and so forth, Brahman alone will grant the result even for the worship of Āditya and the rest, because He is the presiding lord of all;
and this has been explained in the sūtra: "The fruit [comes] from Him, because that is logical" (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.38).

And such is the nature of Brahman’s status as an object of worship here, that it consists in the superimposition of that vision upon the symbols, just as Viṣṇu and others are [superimposed] upon images and the like. // 5 //
The section concerning the meditations on the Āditya and others. Sūtra 6:
And the meditations on the Āditya and others [are to be applied] to the subordinate members [of the sacrifice], because it is appropriate.
"One should meditate upon him who shines yonder as the Udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.1).
"One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1); "One should meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman in speech" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.8.1);
"This [earth] is indeed the Ṛk, fire is the Sāman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1).

Regarding these and other meditations connected with the constituent parts [of the sacrifice], a doubt arises: are the perceptions of the *udgītha* and so forth enjoined upon the sun and so forth, or rather, are the perceptions of the sun and so forth enjoined upon the *udgītha* and so forth?
On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no fixed rule, because there is no cause for such a restriction;
for here, unlike in the case of Brahman, no specific excellence is determined for any one of them, since the entire world is indeed Brahman.
Because it is the cause and because it possesses qualities such as being free from evil, it can be determined to be superior to the sun and other such entities;
however, since the sun and others are equally modifications (vikāra) of the Udgītha and so forth, there is no reason to determine any specific distinction of superiority.
Alternatively, the cognitions of the Udgītha and so forth would necessarily be superimposed upon the sun and other such entities.
Why?
Because the *udgītha* and other such elements consist of action (*karma*), and it is well known that from action the attainment of results follows.
Thus, the sun and other deities, when meditated upon through the conceptions of the *udgītha* and so forth, being of the nature of action, will become the causes of the result.
And likewise, in the passage, "This very *ṛc* is the fire; that is the *sāman*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1), it says, "That *sāman* is superimposed upon this *ṛc*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1).

Here, the word *ṛc* refers to the earth and the word *sāman* refers to the fire. This is appropriate if one intends to effect the meditation (*dṛṣṭi*) of the *ṛc* and *sāman* upon the earth and fire, but not if one were to effect the meditation of the earth and fire upon the *ṛc* and *sāman*.
In the sense of "desire to act":
for the word "king" is applied metaphorically to the charioteer because he performs the functions of a king, but the word "charioteer" is not applied to the king.
Moreover: "One should meditate on the fivefold Sāman in the worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1).
Thus, from the indication of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-nirdeśa*), it is understood that the *sāman* is to be superimposed upon the worlds;
and the passage, "This *gāyatra* is woven upon the vital breaths" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.11.1), shows this very same thing.

Furthermore, in such passages as "The sun is Brahman; this is the instruction" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1), Brahman—which is mentioned last—is superimposed upon the sun and so forth, which are mentioned first.

Likewise, in Vedic texts such as "The earth is the *hiṅkāra* chant" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1), the earth and other elements—which are mentioned first—are [superimposed] upon the *hiṅkāra* and other ritual sounds, which are mentioned last. Therefore...

"The superimposition of a limb upon those that are not limbs, such as the sun and so forth"—this being the position reached, we reply: the cognitions of the sun and so forth are indeed to be superimposed upon the limbs, such as the *udgītha* and so forth. Why? Because it is logical (*upapatti*).

For it is indeed possible that, through a previously unknown connection, there may be an increase in the efficacy of ritual acts when the *udgītha* and other elements are refined by meditations on the sun and so forth.

Furthermore, the text "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), that alone becomes more powerful" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10) shows that knowledge is a cause for the success of ritual acts.
Let it be so in the case of fruits that are the results of ritual actions (*karma*);
but how is it in the case of independent fruits, such as in passages beginning with, "He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold *sāman* among the worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.3)?

Even in those cases, because there is a qualified person (*adhikṛta*) under discussion, it is proper to conceive of a fruit through its proximity to the context (*prakṛta-apūrva*), just like the rule regarding the *godohana* vessel and other such items.

Furthermore, because they consist of the fruit [of action], it is logical that the Sun and others are superior to the *udgītha* and other elements which consist of action; for the fruit of action characterized by the attainment of the Sun and so forth is taught in the Śrutis.
Moreover: "One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1), and "This indeed is the further explanation of that very syllable" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10).
Thus, having introduced the *udgītha* itself as the object of meditation, the text prescribes meditations upon it as being the sun and so forth.
As for the claim that the sun and other deities, when meditated upon through the forms of the *udgītha* and so on, will become the sacrificial action itself and thereby produce the fruit—
that is incorrect.
For it is established that worship itself constitutes an action, and thus its possession of a fruit is logical;
furthermore, even when the *udgītha* and other elements are perceived as being of the nature of the sun and so forth, their essential character as ritual actions does not disappear—as in the passage:
"This *sāman* is superimposed upon this *ṛc*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1).
Thus, the application of the words *ṛk* and *sāman* to the earth and fire is indeed figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).
And figurative usage proceeds, as the case may be, through a connection with its own primary meaning, whether that connection be proximate or remote.
In this regard, although this application of the words *ṛk* and *sāman* occurs in proximity to the earth and fire, it is determined to be due to a connection with the *ṛk* and *sāman* themselves.
For even the word *kṣattṛ*, when applied to a king for some particular reason, cannot be prevented [from being used in that sense];
and the phrase "this very [earth] is the *ṛc*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1), according to the arrangement of its syllables, determines that the earth itself is the *ṛc*.
For if the earth were being determined as the *aktva*, this would merely be a placement of syllables, namely "this very *ṛc*.

Furthermore, the passage, "He who, knowing thus, sings the *sāman*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.7), concludes with a cognition based solely on the subordinate members (*aṅga*), not one based on the earth and so forth.

Likewise, in the passage "One should meditate on the Sāman as fivefold in the worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1), although the worlds are indicated by the locative case, they must nevertheless be superimposed upon the Sāman itself; for it is understood from the accusative indication that the Sāman is the object of meditation.
Indeed, when the worlds are superimposed upon the Sāman, the Sāman becomes meditated upon as having the worlds as its self.
Otherwise, however, the worlds would be worshipped as the self of the *sāman*.
By this, [the passage] beginning with "This *gāyatra* is woven upon the vital breaths" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.11.1) is explained.

Even where there is an identical second instruction—namely, "Now, one should meditate upon this sun as the sevenfold Sāman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.9.1)—there too, it is stated: "Indeed, meditation on the Sāman in its entirety is excellent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.8.1), and likewise regarding the fivefold [Sāman]: "It is excellent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.7.2).

Furthermore, because of the opening statement, "Now, of the sevenfold [Sāman]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.8.1), it is the Sāman itself that is presented as the object of meditation; therefore, the superimposition of the sun and so forth occurs upon that very Sāman.
And precisely from this understanding that the Sāman is the object of meditation, [it follows that] "The earth is the *hiṅkāra*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1).
Even though the instruction is the reverse of such [correspondences], the meditation on earth and so forth must indeed be applied to the *hiṅkāra* and other parts.

Therefore, it is established that the conceptions of the sun and so forth, which do not have those [sun, etc. as their constituent parts (*anaṅga*), should be superimposed upon the constituent parts (*aṅga*) such as the *udgītha*. // 6 //
6. The Topic on Sitting (Āsīnādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 7–10:
"He [should meditate] sitting, because that is possible" (BBs 4.1.7).

First, regarding those meditations connected with the constituent parts of ritual action (*karma*), there is no consideration of sitting and so forth, because they are dependent upon the ritual action itself. Furthermore, in the case of perfect knowledge (*samyagdarśana*), there is likewise no such consideration, because cognition is dependent upon the reality of the object (*vastutantratva*).

Regarding the other meditations (*upāsanā*), however, one considers whether one may proceed while standing, sitting, or lying down without restriction, or whether there is a rule that one must remain seated. On this point, the prima facie view is that because meditation is mental in nature, there is no restriction on the physical posture of the body. To this, the author replies: "One should meditate while seated."
Why? Because of the possibility [of its occurrence].

Meditation (*upāsana*) consists in the production of a continuous flow of identical cognitions, and that is not possible for one who is walking or running, because movement and the like cause distraction of the mind.
Even for one who is standing, the mind occupied with supporting the body is not capable of investigating subtle objects.

Even for one who is lying down, sleep might suddenly overcome him; however, for one who is sitting, such a great defect is easily avoided, and thus it is possible for him to perform the practice. // 7 //

And from meditation (*dhyāna*). Furthermore, one meditates on an object when there is the production of a continuous flow of similar cognitions. And the verb "to meditate" (*dhyāyati*) is seen to be used for those whose bodily movements are relaxed, whose gaze is fixed, and whose minds are drawn toward a single object; as in: "The heron meditates," or "The traveler meditates on his kinsmen."
Moreover, one who is seated remains free from exertion; for this reason also, meditation is an action performed while seated. // 8 //
And it is with reference to immobility.

Furthermore, in the passage, "The earth, as it were, meditates" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.6.1), the expression "meditates" regarding the earth and so forth occurs precisely with reference to their immobility; and that is a mark [indicating] that meditation is an activity performed while sitting. // 9 //
And they remember this;
moreover, the learned remember that posture is an ancillary to meditation, as in [the passage beginning] "Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place" (Gītā 6.11).
For this very reason, specific postures such as the lotus posture (*padmaka*) and others are taught in the Yoga Śāstra. // 10 //
7. One-pointedness is the governing factor. Sūtra 11:
"Where there is one-pointedness, [the result occurs] because there is no distinction.
(BBs 4.1.11) Regarding direction, place, and time, there is a doubt: is there some restrictive rule or not?

To one who might think that because a restriction regarding direction and so forth is observed in most Vedic undertakings, there must likewise be some such restriction here, he says: regarding direction, place, and time, the restriction is determined solely by the purpose; one should meditate precisely where, in whatever direction, place, or time, one-pointedness of mind occurs with ease for oneself. This is because no specific rule is heard—such as "the eastern direction," "forenoon," or "sloping toward the east"—and because the desired one-pointedness is the same everywhere.

But surely some authorities also prescribe specific requirements, as it is said: "In a place that is level, pure, free from gravel, fire, and sand, which is not disturbed by noise or water-bodies, which is agreeable to the mind and does not strain the eyes, one should practice in a cave or a sheltered spot" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.10).
Thus [they argue].
It is said: True, there is indeed such a general rule;
however, since that being the case, there is a specific restriction regarding those [objects] contained therein, the Teacher speaks as a friend:
and this scriptural statement, "favorable to the mind," demonstrates precisely that [concentration occurs] only where one-pointedness exists. // 11 //
8. The Section on Until Death (Āprāyaṇa-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 12:
"Until departure, for that too is seen there.
It was established in the first section that repetition must be observed in all meditations.

In that regard, as for those meditations (*upāsanā*) which have right vision (*samyak-darśana*) as their purpose, it is already known that their limit of repetition is determined by the completion of the task, just like the act of threshing and so forth.
For once the task of right vision has been accomplished, no further effort can be enjoined;
this is because the scripture has no jurisdiction over the realization of one's identity with Brahman, which is not subject to injunction.

Furthermore, regarding those [meditations] that have prosperity as their fruit, this consideration arises: should one cease after practicing the causal condition for some time, or should one practice it throughout one's entire life? What, then, is the initial position? One should abandon it after practicing the causal condition for some time, because the purpose of the term "meditation" (upāsana)—which implies a specific repetition—has been fulfilled.
This being the case, we reply: one should repeat the mental realization until the moment of death, because the attainment of the unseen fruit depends upon the final realization.
For even the karmas, when initiating a fruit to be experienced in another birth, project at the time of death a corresponding consciousness of meditative cultivation (bhāvanāvijñāna).

This is known from such scriptural passages as: "He becomes conscious; he indeed descends with consciousness," and "With whatever mind he comes to the vital breath, that vital breath, joined with heat (tejas), together with the self (ātman), leads him to the world as it has been conceived.
It is also known from the illustration of the caterpillar on the blade of grass.

But these meditations (*pratyaya*), apart from the persistence of their own nature, what else could they require except for the realization through meditation (*bhāvanā-vijñāna*) occurring at the time of death?
Therefore, in those meditations whose essence consists in the realization of the fruit to be attained, there must be repetition until death.
And thus the Śruti says: "Whatever his resolve (*kratu*) was, with that he departs from this world," showing that the meditation persists even at the time of death.

Smṛti also states: "Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having been constantly absorbed in that state" (Gītā 8.6), and also:
"At the time of departure, with an unshaken mind" (Gītā 8.10).
And by the statement, "Therefore, at the time of the end, one should practice these three," it declares that there remains a duty to be performed even at the moment of death. // 12 //
9. That is the section concerning attainment. Sūtra 13:
Upon that attainment, there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the designation thereof.
The third [section], the remainder, is concluded.
Now, an inquiry is undertaken regarding the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
When Brahman is attained, there arises a doubt as to whether that evil (*durita*) which has the opposite result [of liberation] is destroyed or not destroyed.
What, then, is the prima facie position?
Since action exists for the sake of its fruit, its destruction is not possible without the fruit having been given;
for its power to bestow a fruit is established by scripture.
If the fruit were to be exhausted through enjoyment even without that [power], the scripture would be rendered meaningless.
And they remember [the tradition]: "Karma is not exhausted.
But if this is so, does it not follow that the instruction for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) becomes purposeless?
This is not a fault.
This is because expiations are logically established as being occasional (naimittika), like the *iṣṭi* sacrifice performed when a house has caught fire;

moreover, since expiations are prescribed in connection with specific faults, they may indeed serve the purpose of exhausting those faults, but there is no such injunction regarding the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
[Objection: But if the destruction of karma by the knower of Brahman is not admitted, then because the fruit of that karma must necessarily be experienced, there would be no liberation.
It is said: "No.
Liberation will be dependent on place, time, and causal conditions, just like the fruit of ritual action;
therefore, there is no cessation of evil upon the realization of Brahman.

This being the case, we reply: upon that realization—that is, when Brahman is realized—there occurs the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins; namely, the non-clinging of the subsequent and the destruction of the prior.
Why?
Because of the scriptural declaration thereof.

For instance, in the context of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), the scripture declares the non-attachment of future evil that might otherwise be expected for the knower: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.14.3).

Likewise, it declares the destruction even of previously accumulated evil: "Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk thrown into a fire is consumed, even so all his evils are consumed" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.3).
This is another scriptural declaration of the exhaustion of karma: "The knot of the heart is broken; all doubts are cut asunder."
"And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).
As for what was said— that if one assumes the exhaustion of karma whose fruit has not yet been experienced, the scripture would be rendered meaningless—
this fault does not apply.
For we do not deny that action possesses the power to yield its fruit; indeed, that power exists, but we maintain that it is obstructed by other causes such as knowledge (vidyā) and the like.
The scripture functions merely to establish the existence of the capacity [for action], and not with regard to whether there is an obstruction or lack of obstruction.
For even the traditional rule that "karma is not exhausted" is a general principle; it means that karma is not exhausted except through experience, because that is its purpose.

However, its exhaustion through expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and the like is indeed accepted, as in such passages as: "He overcomes all evil," and "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or he who speaks of this very thing, overcomes the murder of a Brahmin."
As for what was said— that these will be occasional expiations—
that is incorrect; for since these [acts], being enjoined in connection with a fault, can have the destruction of that fault as their result, it is illogical to assume any other result.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that there is no injunction for the acquisition of knowledge with the specific aim of destroying defects, as there is in the case of penance—to this we reply:
first of all, such an injunction certainly exists in the case of meditations possessing qualities (*saguṇavidyā*).
And in those cases, the attainment of sovereignty and the cessation of evil are declared for the possessor of that knowledge in the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the texts.
Since there is no reason to disregard these two [passages], it is therefore determined that their fruit is the attainment of sovereignty preceded by the abandonment of evil.

As for the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa), although there is no injunction for it, the destruction of karma is nonetheless established through the realization of the Self as a non-agent. Furthermore, the term "non-adhesion" (aśleṣa) shows that the knower of Brahman does not even assume the state of being an agent with respect to future actions.

But even if, due to false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), one has—as it were—assumed agency with respect to those [past actions] that have already passed away, nevertheless, because false knowledge is sublated through the power of true knowledge (*vidyā*), those [actions] also dissolve; thus he says "destruction.
For the nature of non-agency and non-enjoyment throughout all three times is the opposite of the previously established states of agency and enjoyership.
The knower of Brahman realizes: "I am Brahman; neither previously nor now, nor even in the future time, was I a doer or an enjoyer.
In this very way, liberation becomes possible.

For otherwise, in the absence of the exhaustion of karmas that have been operating since beginningless time, there would be no liberation. Furthermore, liberation cannot be dependent on place, time, or causes in the manner of the fruit of karma,
because that would entail the consequence of its being impermanent.
And because being beyond the senses is untenable, [the result] is knowledge;
therefore, it is certain that upon the realization of Brahman, there is the destruction of evil. 13.
10. The Section on Non-Attachment to Other [Sins] (Itarāsaṃśleṣādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 14:
"In the same way, there is non-attachment for the other as well; but at death.

In the preceding section, it was established on the basis of scriptural instruction that the non-attachment and destruction of natural sin—which is the cause of bondage—are brought about by knowledge.

Furthermore, since merit (*dharma*) is scriptural in nature, one might suspect that there is no contradiction with scriptural knowledge; anticipating this, the principle of the preceding section is extended here in order to refute that view.
For the other [type of action], namely meritorious karma, there is likewise non-clinging and destruction for the possessor of knowledge, just as in the case of sin.
Why? Because, since that too has its own fruit as its cause, it would follow that it acts as an obstacle to the fruit of knowledge.

Furthermore, in such scriptural passages as "He indeed crosses over both of these" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), there is a mention of the destruction of good deeds (*sukṛta*) just as there is of evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*);

and because the destruction of karma—which is caused by the realization of the Self as a non-agent—is equal for both good and evil deeds, [it is said]: "And his actions are exhausted" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).
And this is because of the scriptural statement that makes no distinction.
Even where the word "evil" (pāpman) is seen alone, it should be understood that by that very term, merit (puṇya) as well is included,
since its fruit is inferior when compared to the fruit of knowledge.
Moreover, the word "evil" (*pāpman*) is used even for merit (*puṇya*) in the Śruti: "Day and night do not cross this bridge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.1).

Here, after mentioning both what is well-done and what is ill-done together, it is stated that "all evils turn back from here"; thus, because the word "evil" is employed without distinction for the merit under discussion, [the term applies to both].
As for the phrase "at the falling away," the word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of emphasis.

Thus, since the non-clinging and destruction of merit and demerit—the causes of bondage—are established through the power of knowledge, he concludes that liberation for the wise person is inevitable upon the falling away of the body. // 14 //
11. Topic: That which has not yet begun to bear fruit. Sūtra 15:
"But only those [deeds] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], for that is the limit.
(BBs 4.1.15) In the two preceding topics, it was established that the destruction of good and evil deeds is caused by knowledge. Does that [destruction] apply to all of them? Or...

It is now considered whether [the destruction of karma] applies without distinction to both those whose effects have begun (*ārabdhakārya*) and those whose effects have not yet begun (*anārabdhakārya*), or whether it applies specifically only to those whose effects have not yet begun.
In this regard, because such scriptural passages as "He indeed crosses over both of these" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22) state it without distinction, the destruction occurs without distinction.

This being the case, he replies: "But only those whose effects have not yet begun. That is to say, only those previously accumulated in other lives, and those accumulated in this life prior to the arising of knowledge—provided their fruits have not yet commenced—are destroyed by the attainment of knowledge; however, those whose effects have already begun—that is, those whose fruits have been partially experienced—are not destroyed.

By which two this birth, the locus of the knowledge of Brahman, was fashioned—whence is this known? From the scriptural passage, "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2), because the attainment of security occurs upon the falling away of the body.
Otherwise, if all karma were destroyed by knowledge, then in the absence of any cause for continued existence, one would attain liberation immediately upon the acquisition of knowledge;
in that case, he would not have taught the waiting for the fall of the body.
But surely, by the very force of reality, this realization of the self as a non-agent, while exhausting karmas, would exhaust some and yet overlook others?

For it cannot be maintained that, when the contact with fire and seed is equal, the potency of the seed is destroyed in some cases but not destroyed in others. To this it is replied: First of all, the arising of knowledge is not possible without depending upon the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) whose effects have already begun. And once that [deposit] has been relied upon, just as in the case of a potter’s wheel, because an obstruction in the interval is impossible for that which has set in motion, there remains the maintenance of the momentum until its exhaustion.
For even the realization of the Self as a non-agent destroys karmas by subverting false knowledge;
yet, even though it has been subverted, false knowledge continues for some time due to the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), just like the cognition of two moons.
Furthermore, one should not dispute here whether or not the body of the knower of Brahman is maintained for some time.
For how could another possibly refute both the realization of Brahman—which is a matter of conviction in one's own heart—and the maintenance of the body by a single person?
Moreover, this very point is explained through the description of the characteristics of one whose wisdom is steadfast (*sthitaprajña*) in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.
Therefore, the conclusion is that only those good and evil deeds whose effects have not yet begun are destroyed by the power of knowledge. // 15 //

12. Section on the Agnihotra and other rites. Sūtras 16–17: "But the Agnihotra and so forth are for that very purpose (liberation), because it is seen [in scripture]. Having raised the doubt that the principle of the non-clinging and destruction of merit—just as in the case of sin—is extended by analogy to all merit, the author replies: "But the Agnihotra and so forth... The principle of the non-clinging and destruction of sin has been extended by analogy to merit as well. Anticipating the objection that this extension applies to all merit whatsoever, he answers with the words: "But the Agnihotra and so forth. This indicates that while the rule regarding sin applies to all other merits, it does not apply to the Agnihotra and similar obligatory rites. This is because such rites are seen in scripture to lead directly to liberation. Thus, the Agnihotra and other such works are indeed conducive to that same goal. Furthermore, since these rites are performed without attachment to results, they do not cling to the soul; rather, through their purification of the mind, they become instrumental in attaining the knowledge of Brahman. Therefore, they are not destroyed like other merits, but rather serve as a means to the realization of the Self. Hence, the Agnihotra and other such rites are for that very purpose. This concludes the section. (Sūtra 16) Regarding the statement "because it is seen," the meaning is that it is observed in the scriptures that those who perform the Agnihotra and other such rites, when combined with knowledge, attain the supreme goal. For example, the scripture says: "Those who, performing sacrifices and penances, worship me with faith, they too have come to me" (Gītā 9.25). Moreover, the scripture shows that the Agnihotra and other rites are not obstacles to knowledge, but rather its auxiliaries. As it is said: "One should perform actions here without attachment for the purification of the self" (Gītā 5.10). Therefore, the Agnihotra and other rites are for that very purpose of liberation. This concludes the section. (Sūtra 17)
The word "tu" (but) dispels a doubt.

The meaning is that whatever Vedic obligatory rite (*nitya-karma*), such as the *agnihotra* and so forth, has as its purpose—that very same purpose belongs to this [knowledge] as well; that which is the effect of knowledge is indeed its effect too.
Why? Because of such scriptural indications as: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, and by charity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Now, an objection may be raised: since knowledge and action have distinct effects, their unity in a single effect is untenable.
This is not a fault;
for even in the case of the effects of fever and death, when curd and poison are combined with molasses and mantras respectively, the effects of satisfaction and nourishment are observed.
Likewise, it is logical that action, when conjoined with knowledge, can have liberation as its effect.
But surely liberation is not something to be undertaken; how then can it be said to be the effect of action?
This is not a fault, because action is helpful from afar.
For it is right action alone that leads to knowledge, and thus it is figuratively described as the cause of liberation through the life-channel (*prāṇāḍī*).
For this very reason, this statement regarding the unity of the effect refers to a transcended object;
for indeed, for one who knows Brahman, future rites such as the *agnihotra* are no longer possible.

Because the realization of Brahman as the Self—which is beyond all injunctions—is not within the scope of the scripture; whereas in the case of meditations involving qualities (*saguṇavidyā*), since agency has not ceased, future rites such as the *agnihotra* are possible. Even for those [rites], because they are performed without desire for rewards and have no other purpose, their connection with knowledge (*vidyā*) is established. // 16 //

But with reference to what subject is this statement regarding non-attachment and destruction made, or with reference to what subject is that statement of certain reciters of the Veda regarding the distribution of rewards: "His sons inherit his property; his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds"?
To this, he reads the following reply:
"For some, there is also another of both.

(BBs 4.1.17) For, besides that obligatory rite such as the *agnihotra*, there is indeed another "good deed" (*sādhukṛtyā*) performed with a view toward its fruit; regarding this, the application has been stated by certain followers of a Vedic branch: "Friends attain the good deeds."
And this determination regarding the non-clinging and destruction of that very [sin], as in the case of "aghavat," applies to other [sins] as well, such that there is no clinging [to them].
Thus, both teachers, Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa, are in agreement regarding the fact that such optional (kāmya) action does not assist knowledge. 17.
Section 13: The Topic on the Means for the Accomplishment of Knowledge (vidyā) and Wisdom (jñāna). Sūtra 18:
"For [it is said], 'by knowledge alone'.
This has been established in the immediately preceding section that the obligatory rites such as the Agnihotra must be performed by one seeking liberation (mumukṣu) for the purpose of liberation.
That which is performed as a prescribed duty (uddeśa), by way of being a cause for the destruction of previously acquired demerit, becomes a means for the purification of the self;
thus, by serving as a cause for attaining Brahman—the ultimate purpose of liberation—it becomes a single-purpose activity together with the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā).
In this regard, there exists both karma such as the Agnihotra that is conjoined with knowledge based on its constituent parts (aṅga), and that which is independent (kevala).

"He who, knowing thus, sacrifices"; "He who, knowing thus, offers oblations"; "He who, knowing thus, recites"; "He who, knowing thus, sings"; "Therefore, let one make only him who knows thus the Brahman priest, and not one who does not know thus" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.17.10); "By that, both perform [the rite]: he who knows this thus, and he who does not know it" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10).
From such statements as these, it follows that ritual action conjoined with knowledge exists, and that it also exists independently.

In this regard, the following is investigated: does only the Agnihotra and other rites conjoined with knowledge serve as a cause for liberation for one seeking release by attaining a single purpose together with that knowledge, and not those performed independently; or do both—those conjoined with knowledge and those performed independently—equally [serve as causes] without distinction?

Whence arises this doubt? It arises from the scriptural statement, "They desire to know this very Self through sacrifice," which teaches that sacrifices and the like are, without exception, auxiliary means to the knowledge of the Self;
and because it is understood that the Agnihotra and other rites possess no distinction when conjoined with knowledge.

What, then, is the prima facie view? That ritual action such as the Agnihotra attains the status of being an auxiliary to the knowledge of the Self only when conjoined with knowledge, and not when devoid of knowledge.
This is because one who is endowed with knowledge is understood to be superior to one devoid of knowledge,
according to such scriptural passages as: "On whatever day he offers [the oblation], on that very day he who knows thus conquers rebirth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1),
and "The intellect, O Pārtha, by which you shall cast off the bondage of action" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.39).
"And from such Smṛti passages as: 'For action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom, O Dhanañjaya' (Gītā 2.49).
This being the position reached, the author replies: "For [it is said], 'Whatever one does with knowledge... etc.
This is true:
ritual action such as the *agnihotra*, when conjoined with knowledge, is superior to ritual action devoid of knowledge—just as a learned Brāhmaṇa is superior to a Brāhmaṇa devoid of learning.
Nevertheless, ritual action such as the *agnihotra* that is devoid of knowledge is not entirely disregarded.
Why? Because it is heard in scripture without qualification that the Agnihotra and other rites are causes of knowledge, in the passage: "They desire to know this very Self by means of sacrifice.

Now, one might argue: since it is understood that the Agnihotra and other rites when conjoined with knowledge are superior to those devoid of knowledge, it is logical that the Agnihotra and other rites devoid of knowledge are simply not required as causes for the knowledge of the Self.
This is not so.

It is reasonable to assume that for one who possesses knowledge as an auxiliary, the Agnihotra and other rites— due to their conjunction with an excellence of capacity caused by knowledge— will possess a certain superiority as a cause toward self-knowledge, whereas this is not the case for one devoid of knowledge. However, it is not possible to maintain that the Agnihotra and other rites, which are heard in the text "They desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*) as being limbs of self-knowledge without distinction, lack the status of being such limbs.
For thus says the Śruti: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣadic insight—that alone becomes more powerful" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10).

By declaring that ritual acts such as the Agnihotra become more powerful when conjoined with knowledge, this passage—speaking of a certain excellence regarding their own effects—demonstrates that those very same acts, when devoid of knowledge, lack that power toward their intended purpose.
And the potency of action consists in its power to accomplish its own purpose;
therefore, both the obligatory *agnihotra* and other rites— whether conjoined with knowledge or devoid of knowledge— whatever has been performed by one seeking liberation for the sake of liberation,
in this life or in another birth prior to the arising of knowledge, that [action] [bears fruit] according to its capacity.

It is established that the means which serve as the cause for attaining Brahman—by way of being the cause for the destruction of accumulated sins that obstruct the realization of Brahman—attain the status of a cause for the realization of Brahman by depending on internal causes such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), faith (*śraddhā*), and intentness (*tātparya*); thus, they share a single effect with the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). // 18 //
14. Section on the Destruction of the Other. Sūtra 19:
"But having exhausted the others through experience, he then attains [Brahman].

(BBs 4.1.19) It has been stated that the destruction of merit and demerit whose effects have not yet begun occurs through the power of knowledge; however, as for the others—namely, those whose effects have already begun—[their exhaustion occurs] through experience.

This is because of such scriptural passages as: "Having exhausted merit and demerit through experience, one attains Brahman; for him there is delay only so long as he is not released, then he shall be merged" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2), and "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman," and others like these.

[Objection: Even when right vision (*samyagdarśana*) exists, just as the perception of duality persists prior to the fall of the body according to the analogy of seeing two moons, so too would it persist thereafter. [Reply:
No, because of the absence of a cause.
For in that case, the persistence is caused by the exhaustion of remaining karmic experiences (*upabhogaśeṣa*); and such a thing no longer exists.
[Objection: But will another latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) not begin a new experience?
[Reply: No, because its seed has been burnt.
For it is only another karma, supported by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), that initiates a further experience upon the fall of the body; and that false knowledge [is likewise destroyed].

For an action that serves as a support initiates another experience upon the fall of the body; however, since that false knowledge has been burnt away by right knowledge, it is well said that when the commenced effects are exhausted, liberation necessarily occurs for the wise one. // 19 //
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
The second quarter of the fourth chapter. In this quarter, there is an investigation into the departure and the journey [of the soul].
1. Section on Speech (Vāg-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 1–2:
"Speech [is merged] in the mind, because it is so seen [in scripture] and because of the sacred word.
Now, desiring to introduce the path of the gods for the attainment of results in other meditations, [the author] first explains the sequence of departure according to the scriptures.
For the author will state that the departure of the knower and the ignorant is indeed the same:

there is a scriptural passage concerning the time of death which says, "Of this person, my dear, when he is departing, speech merges into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into fire, and fire into the supreme deity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6).
Here there is a doubt: is it said that speech itself, as something possessing activity, merges into the mind, or is it the activity of speech [that merges]?
In this regard, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that speech itself merges into the mind;
for in that way, the scriptural statement is supported.
Otherwise, there would be a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And when there is no distinction between direct denotation (*śruti*) and metaphorical indication, direct denotation is the more reasonable, not metaphorical indication.
Therefore, this dissolution of speech itself occurs in the mind.
This being the case, we reply: although it has been explained that speech is a function, the Teacher actually reads the text as "speech [merges] in the mind.
This is true;
however, he will later state, "There is non-division, because of the scriptural statement" (Brahma-sūtra 4.2.16).
Therefore, it is understood that here what is intended is merely the cessation of activity (*vṛtty-upaśama*).

If, however, the intention were the dissolution into the ultimate reality (*tattva-pralaya*), then since there would be an identical state of non-distinction everywhere, why specify "non-distinction" only in relation to the Supreme?
Therefore, the intention here is the withdrawal of activity.
The meaning is that the activity of speech is withdrawn first while the activity of the mind remains present.
Why?
Because it is so observed.
For it is observed that the withdrawal of the function of speech occurs even while the function of the mind is still present.
Now, it was argued that by the force of the scriptural statement, this dissolution of speech alone into the mind is logical;
[to this] he says: "No."
Because it does not have that as its material cause.
For when something originates from a particular source, its dissolution into that source is logical, just as a clay vessel dissolves into clay;
however, there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever to show that speech originates from the mind.
However, the emergence and suppression of functions are observed even when they do not rely on their own material cause (*aprakṛti*).
For instance, the function of the fiery element, fire, emerges from fuel consisting of earthy substances, and it subsides within water.
How, then, is it that in this view [of yours] it is said that "speech merges into the mind"?
Therefore, he says: "And from scripture" (*śabdāt ca*).

The meaning is that even the scriptural statement is consistent with this position, because of the metaphorical treatment of the non-difference between the function (*vṛtti*) and that which possesses the function (*vṛttimat*). // 1 // [FN:
Of one who is striving at the time of death.]
And for this very reason, all [the senses] follow [the soul]: "Therefore, with its heat calmed,
it enters again into a new existence through the senses merging into the mind" (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.9).
Thus, here it is heard that the dissolution of all the sense organs without distinction occurs in the mind.

In that regard, for the same reason as with speech— since the cessation of function is observed in the case of the eyes and other organs when the mind remains with its functions intact, and since their essential nature cannot possibly dissolve and the scriptural statement is thus consistent— it follows that all the sense organs follow after the mind by way of their functions alone.

Since the withdrawal of all the organs into the mind occurs without distinction, the separate mention of speech—stating that "speech is merged into the mind"—is made in accordance with the specific example [given in the scripture]. // 2 //
The section concerning the mind. Sūtra 3:
That mind [merges] into the vital breath, because of what follows. It has been established that "speech merges into the mind" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6).
Thus, in this case, it was intended that there is the merging of the functions.
Now, regarding the subsequent statement, "The mind [merges] in breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6),

when a doubt arises as to whether here too the merging of the functions alone is intended, or the merging of the possessor of the functions, the prima facie view is that here it is indeed the merging of the possessor of the functions.
This is because it is supported by scripture and because its being composed of that [element] is logically established.

For instance, [the Chāndogya Upaniṣad states]: "For, my dear, the mind consists of food, and the vital breath consists of water" (Chā. 6.5.4); thus, it declares the mind to have food as its source and the vital breath to have water as its source.
The Śruti states: "And the waters created food.
Therefore, it follows that the mind is merged into the vital breath (prāṇa) because of the non-difference between the material cause and its modification.

This being the position reached, we reply: even that mind, when its external sensory functions have ceased, is merged into the vital breath solely by way of its own mental modifications; this is to be understood from the subsequent passage.

For instance, in one who is about to fall asleep or is on the verge of death, while the vital function (*prāṇavṛtti*) consisting of movement remains present, the cessation of the mental functions (*manovṛtti*) is observed; yet,
the dissolution of the mind's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) into the vital breath is not possible, because the mind does not have that as its material cause (*prakṛti*).
Now, it was indeed shown that the mind has the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its material cause (*prakṛti*).
This, however, is not sound.
For the mind cannot be said to merge into the vital breath by virtue of such a derivative causal relationship.
For even in this way, the mind would merge into food, and food into water, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) [would merge] into water;

yet, even in this alternative view, there is no authority whatsoever for the claim that the mind is born from water that has been transformed into the state of the vital breath. Therefore, there is no merging of the mind’s own nature (*svarūpa*) into the vital breath.

Rather, the word [“merges”] is appropriate even in the case of the merging of the function (*vṛtti*), because it has been shown that the identity of the function and the possessor of the function is treated as non-different through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). //3//
3. The Section on the Overseer (Adhyakṣa-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 4–6. Sūtra 4:
"That [subtle body] [merges] with the overseer, because of its approaching him and so forth.

It has been established that when something does not originate from another, its functional absorption (vṛttipralaya) into that other does not imply the destruction of its own essential nature (svarūpapralaya).

Now this is considered: regarding the statement "the breath [merges] into heat," does the function and withdrawal of the breath occur into heat alone according to the scriptural text, or rather into the individual soul (jīva), who is the presiding lord over the cage of the body and senses?
In this regard, because the scriptural text is not to be doubted, the merging of the breath must occur into heat alone, as it is improper to assume what is not stated in scripture.
This being the case, it is established that "he" is the presiding overseer (*adhyakṣa*).
That aforementioned vital breath (*prāṇa*) abides in the conscious self (*vijñānātman*), which is conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*), karma, and prior cognition (*pūrvaprajñā*).
The meaning is that the function of the vital breath becomes subordinate to that [conscious self].

Why? Because of the scriptural passages concerning "approaching" and so forth. For another Vedic text—namely, "At the time of death, all the vital breaths (prāṇas) gather around this very self, when one becomes one who breathes upwards"—shows without distinction that all the prāṇas approach the presiding deity (adhyakṣa).

And specifically, the passage "When he departs, the prāṇa departs after him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2) shows that the fivefold prāṇa follows its presiding deity, and that the others follow it in turn;
as it says, "When the prāṇa departs, all the vital breaths depart after it."
