And by the statement, "He becomes endowed with consciousness," which demonstrates that the presiding soul (adhyakṣa) possesses internal consciousness, it indicates that the vital breath (prāṇa), whose collection of organs has been absorbed, remains within that soul.

Now, an objection may be raised: since scripture states that "the breath [merges] into heat" (tejas), how can the breath be said to be in the presiding soul? This is an unwarranted addition. To this we reply: this is not a fault.

Because the empirical usage of "departing" and so forth is primarily based on the presiding deity (adhyakṣa), and because even the specific details found in other scriptural passages must be taken into account. // 4 //

How then is the scriptural statement "the vital breath [merges] into heat" to be understood? To this he says: "In the elements, because of that scriptural statement" (BBs 4.2.5). It should be understood that the presiding soul, conjoined with the vital breath, abides in the subtle elements—which are the seeds of the body and which accompany heat.
"Prāṇa [merges] into heat," so says the Śruti.
But is it not the case that this Śruti shows the abiding of prāṇa alone in heat, and not of the presiding soul (adhyakṣa) conjoined with prāṇa?
This is not a fault.
"He [is] the presiding officer (adhyakṣa)"—because this term has also been included as an intermediate case for the presiding officer.
For even one who, having gone from Srughna to Mathurā, proceeds from Mathurā to Pāṭaliputra, can also be said to "go from Srughna to Pāṭaliputra.

Therefore, in the phrase "the breath (prāṇa) [merges] into heat (tejas)," this refers to the abiding of the presiding officer himself, conjoined with the breath, within the elements that accompany that heat. // 5 //
How is it that [the soul] is said to be among the elements accompanied by fire, when it is heard only once, namely, "the breath [merges] into fire"?
To this he says: "Not into one, for [the two scriptures] show [this]. (BBs 4.2.6)

The individual soul does not abide in fire alone at the time of seeking another body, because it is observed that the body to be produced consists of multiple elements. This point is demonstrated by the question and answer regarding "the waters having the form of a person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3). That has been explained here under the sūtra: "But [it is] threefold, on account of the predominance [of water]" (Brahma-sūtra 3.1.2).
Both Śruti and Smṛti demonstrate this point.
Śruti says: "Consisting of earth, consisting of water, consisting of air, consisting of ether, consisting of fire," and so forth.
Smṛti also says: "The subtle, imperishable particles of which the five elements are said to consist..."
"Along with these, all this comes into being in due succession," and so forth.

Now, when the organs such as speech have been withdrawn at the time of seeking another body, another Śruti passage—beginning with "What then becomes of this person? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13)—determines that action (*karman*) is the substratum: "Whatever those two said, they said it was indeed action; and whatever they praised, they praised it as indeed action."
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13).

To this it is replied: In that [passage], the dependence on karma was stated because the operation of bondage—which consists of the senses and their objects and is designated as "grasps" (graha) and "over-grasps" (atigraha)—is impelled by karma.
Here, however, the dependence on the elements (bhūta) is stated because the production of another body occurs through the appropriation of the elements.
Even from the word "praise" (*praśaṃsā*), only the predominance of the action (*karman*) is indicated therein, but another substratum (*āśraya*) is not excluded;
therefore, there is no contradiction. // 6 // [FN: Of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*), which are the fivefold (*daśārdha*).]
The *aṇvyaḥ* are subtle; they are called *mātrāḥ* because they are measured (*mīyante*). Section 4: On the Beginning of the Course. Sūtra 7.
"And equal [to all], until the commencement of the path, and immortality without having burned away [the body].

(BBs 4.2.7) Regarding this departure (*utkrānti*), for those who are in doubt as to whether it is common to both the knower and the ignorant or whether it possesses distinctions, the initial position reached is that it possesses distinctions;
for this [departure] is characterized by its dependence on the elements (*bhūta*).
Furthermore, living beings depend upon [the senses] for rebirth;
yet rebirth does not occur for the wise man.
For it is an established principle that "the wise man attains immortality."
Therefore, this departure belongs only to the ignorant person. But is it not the case that, because it is mentioned within the context of knowledge (*vidyā*), it must belong to the knower? No;
for it is a mere restatement of what occurs naturally, just like the state of deep sleep and so forth.

For thus, in the passage, "When this person is said to sleep," "when he is said to hunger," and "when he is said to thirst" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.3, 5), sleep and so forth— which are common to all living beings— are merely mentioned; even though they occur within the context of knowledge (*vidyā*), it is for the purpose of illustrating the reality intended to be established, and not because these states are intended to be prescribed as specific attributes of the knower.

Thus, this departure (*utkrānti*) is described only with reference to the common people, in order to establish that "That which is the Supreme Deity into which the light of a person striving for perfection merges—that Self is the Reality; Thou art That. Furthermore, this departure is denied for the man of knowledge in the passage: "His vital breaths do not depart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).
Therefore, this [departure] belongs only to the ignorant.

This being the position reached, we reply: this departure—beginning with "Speech merges into the mind" and so forth—is common to both the wise and the ignorant until the commencement of the journey (āsṛti), because there is no scriptural statement to the contrary.

Impelled by karma, [the soul] transmigrates, taking recourse to the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) which are the seeds of the body and are non-contradictory [to its state], in order to experience the assumption of a body.
The knower (*vidvān*), however, takes recourse to the door of the channel of liberation (*mokṣanāḍīdvāra*) illuminated by knowledge.
This very point has been stated [in the sūtra] as "beginning from the path of transmigration" (*āsṛti upakramāt*).

Now, it may be objected: "Immortality is indeed what must be attained by the knower, and that is not dependent upon another place; therefore, why should there be a resort to the elements or a departure on a path? To this it is replied: Without having burned away—that is, without having utterly consumed—the afflictions such as ignorance through the power of lower knowledge (aparavidyā), one seeks a relative immortality; for such a person, a departure on a path and a resort to the elements are possible.
For the movement of life-breaths that are without a support is not possible;
therefore, there is no fault. // 7 //
5. The Section on the Designation of Saṃsāra. Sūtra 8–11:
*Tadāpīteḥ saṃsāravyapadeśāt* (Because of the designation of saṃsāra until that [re-absorption]).
"The fire [is merged] in the highest deity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6).

Thus, here by the force of the context, it is stated that that very fire— as it has been under discussion— along with the presiding deity, along with the vital breath, along with the collection of organs, and accompanied by the other elements, becomes merged into the highest divinity for the person who is departing. Now, it is considered what kind of merging this might be.
In that case, it follows first of all that there is an absolute dissolution of its own nature;
for it has been established that the Supreme Deity is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the entire multitude of things subject to birth. This is because such a status is logically consistent.
Therefore, this attainment of non-distinction is absolute.

This being the position reached, we reply: that subtle essence of the elements, such as fire and the rest, which serves as the substratum for the instruments of perception like the ear, persists until final dissolution—that is, until liberation from saṃsāra through the cause of perfect knowledge. As it is said: "Some embodied beings enter a womb for the sake of a body..."
This is because of the description of transmigratory existence in such passages as, "Some follow the post, according to their karma and according to their learning" (KaU 5.7).
For otherwise, everyone would attain absolute union with Brahman at the very moment of death, due to the dissolution of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
In that case, the scriptures of injunction and the scriptures of knowledge would be purposeless;
furthermore, bondage, which has its cause in false knowledge, cannot be loosened except through right knowledge.
Therefore, even though it is their original nature, this merging remains as a mere state of seed-potential, like deep sleep or cosmic dissolution. // 8 //
And it is subtle by measure, because it is perceived as such.
Furthermore, that fire, accompanied by the other elements, which serves as the substratum for the soul departing from this body, must be subtle both in its essential nature and in its measure.
For its subtlety is perceived from such [scriptural] indications as the departure through the channels (*nāḍī*).
In that regard, its movement is possible because of its subtlety;
its lack of resistance is possible because of its transparency.
For this very reason, it is not perceived by those standing nearby when it emerges from the body. // 9 //
"Not by destruction, therefore.
(BBs 4.2.10) For this very reason, because of its subtlety, the other subtle body does not perish through the destruction of this gross body caused by burning and so forth. // 10 //
And from this very same reasoning follows its heat (ūṣman).
This heat belongs to that very subtle body, which they perceive as warmth through touch within this physical body.
For it is observed that even in the state of death, while the body remains and its qualities such as form and so forth persist, [the heat is absent].

Heat is not perceived [in the body] when it is dead, but it is indeed perceived while in the state of being alive; therefore, since heat is not perceived among the qualities of the body but is perceived only during the state of life, it follows that this heat has its locus in something distinct from the well-known body.
And thus says the Śruti: "One who is warm shall live; one who is cold shall die. (11)
6. The Section on Prohibition (Pratiṣedha-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 12–14.
"If it be argued that [there is no departure] because of the prohibition, we say no, because [the prohibition refers only] to the embodied soul" (BBs 4.2.12).
From this qualification, namely "and immortality without having burned away [the body]," it is accepted that in the case of absolute immortality, there is an absence of both movement and departure.

If it be argued that even in that case, having raised the suspicion of departure for some reason, [the text] prohibits it—stating: "Now, he who does not desire, who is without desire, free from desire, whose desire is attained, whose desire is the Self—for him the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) do not depart; being Brahman, he merges into Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upani�sad 4.4.6)—and therefore, because of this prohibition concerning the subject of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), there is no departure of the vital breaths from the body for the knower of the supreme Brahman.
It is said: "No.
For this prohibition of the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) refers to the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*), not to the body.
How is this understood? From the use of the ablative case in another recensional text (*śākhāntara*), namely: "From him the vital breaths do not depart" (*na tasmāt prāṇā utkrāmanti*).
For the genitive case, which has the general relation as its object, is restricted to a specific relation by the ablative case occurring in another Vedic branch.

And because of its predominance, it is the embodied soul—the subject entitled to prosperity and the supreme good—who is connected [as the one departing], not the body. No; the meaning is that from the living self (jīva) desiring to depart, the vital breaths (prāṇas) depart along with it. // 12 //
And for one who possesses vital breath and is departing on a journey, there is an "exit" from the body. This being the position reached, it is replied:
"For it is clear to some.
(BBs 4.2.13) That which was stated—that even for the knower of the supreme Brahman there is exit from the body because the prohibition of exit has the body as its basis—is not so.
For the denial of departure is clearly perceived by some reciters as referring specifically to the body as the substrate;

for instance, in the question of Ārtabhāga: "When this person dies, do the vital breaths depart from him or not? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.11), to which Yājñavalkya replied: "No," he said. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.11)
Having thus adopted the position that there is no departure [of the vital breaths], one might raise the objection: "In that case, this person does not die while the vital breaths have not departed.

To address this doubt, it is asserted that the vital breaths are dissolved right here, and for the sake of establishing that, it is stated: "He swells up, is inflated internally, and lies dead, bloated" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.11).
Thus, they record the swelling and so forth as the limits of departure for that which is under discussion and is referred to by the word "it"—
and these [phenomena] would belong to the body, not to the embodied soul.

On account of that similarity, in the passage "The vital breaths do not depart from him; they are merged right here," even here, by means of figurative identification (*upacāra*), there is a prohibition of departure having the body as its point of origin. Even if it were explained that the embodied self is primary—according to those who read the ablative case (*pañcamī*)—for those, however, who read the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), it would follow that the departure belonging to the knower is prohibited; yet, since the purpose of this sentence is to prohibit departure, that [departure] must have the body as its point of origin.
The departure from the body is thus prohibited; it belongs to the embodied being, not to the Self.

Furthermore: "When he departs—whether through the eye, or through the head, or through other parts of the body—the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him; when the vital breath departs, all the vital breaths depart after it" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad).

Thus, having demonstrated in detail the departure and the journey through transmigratory existence as pertaining to the ignorant, and having concluded the discourse on the ignorant with the words, "Thus indeed is he who desires" (Bṛ. 4.4.6), the text designates the knower with the words, "But now, he who does not desire" (Bṛ.
4.4.6). If, even in that case regarding the knower, one were to admit a departure [of the soul], this designation would be entirely inconsistent.

Therefore, it must be explained in this very way that the departure (*gati*) and the exit from the body (*utkrānti*), which apply to those who are not possessed of knowledge, are prohibited in the case of the knower, so that the scriptural designation may be meaningful.

Furthermore, for the knower of Brahman—who has become the all-pervading Self of Brahman and whose desires and karmas have been exhausted—neither exit nor departure is possible due to the absence of a cause.
Scriptural passages such as "Here one attains Brahman" likewise indicate the non-existence of both departure and exit. // 13 //
And it is also recorded in tradition;

furthermore, the absence of both a destination and a departure is recorded in the *Mahābhārata*: "Even the gods are bewildered regarding the path of one who has become the self of all beings, who perceives all beings correctly, and who is trackless while those seek his tracks."

Is it not recorded in the Smṛti that for one who knows Brahman—who has become the Self of Brahman, which is omnipresent—a "going" occurs? For instance, it is said that Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, desiring liberation, set out toward the solar orb; and when called back by his father who followed him, he replied, "Bho!
No; this must be understood as the casting off of the body by one who is still embodied, preceded by the attainment of a specific location through the power of yoga.
Because of the mention of being visible to all beings and so forth;
for indeed, all beings would not be able to see one who is bodiless while moving.
And thus it is concluded in that very context: "But Śuka, having attained a speed swifter than the wind, traveled through the atmosphere."
"Having displayed his own power, he became one who has gone to all beings.

Therefore, for the knower of the Supreme Brahman, there is non-existence as the destination in both departure and [the state after death]. As for the subject matter of the scriptural texts concerning "going," we shall explain it later. // 14 //

Section 7: The Dissolution of Speech and the Other Senses. Sūtra 15: "They [merge] into That, for so it says. (BBs 4.2.15) Furthermore, those senses and elements denoted by the term *prāṇa* merge into that very Supreme Self of the knower of the Supreme Brahman.
Why?
Because the Śruti says: "In this very way, these sixteen parts of the observer, which have the Puruṣa as their goal, reach the Puruṣa and dissolve" (Praśna 6.5).
But is it not said: "The fifteen parts have gone to their respective foundations" (Muṇḍaka 3.2.7)?
Thus, another scriptural passage concerning the enlightened person indeed states that the dissolution of the constituent parts (*kalā*) occurs elsewhere than in the Supreme Self. [Reply: No;

for that passage is with reference to conventional usage, meaning that the constituent parts such as earth and so forth simply return to their own respective primal sources, such as earth and so forth.
The other [text], however, refers to the realization of the knower:
for one who knows the Supreme Brahman, the entire collection of parts becomes Brahman itself.
Therefore, there is no fault. // 15 //
8. The Section on Non-Differentiation. Sūtra 16:
"There is non-differentiation, because of the scriptural statement.
(BBs 4.2.16) Furthermore, regarding this dissolution of the parts for the wise one, does it occur with a remainder like that of others, or rather without a remainder?
In this regard, since it might follow from the commonality of dissolution that only the *śakti* remains, he says: "It is simply the attainment of non-distinction.
Why? Because of the scriptural statement.

For, after describing the dissolution of the *kalās*, [the scripture] says: "Their names and forms are destroyed; he is called simply 'Puruṣa'; he becomes partless and immortal" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.5).
Furthermore, it is not logical that the constituent parts (kalās), which have ignorance as their cause, should remain with a residue during dissolution, which has knowledge as its cause;
therefore, there is indeed non-differentiation. // 16 //
9. That abode is the locus. Sūtra 17:

"The flaming up of that abode, the door being illumined by it, through the power of knowledge and through the application of recollection of the path which is its remainder, [the soul] is favored by the one within the heart by means of the hundred-and-first [vein].
(BBs 4.2.17) The incidental discussion concerning the path of higher knowledge is concluded.
Now he continues the consideration of the subject matter of the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*).
It has been stated that the departure of both the knower and the ignorant is the same from the beginning of the process; he now demonstrates that process starting from the point of death.

For that self of consciousness (*vijñānātman*) who is about to depart and whose aggregate of speech and other faculties has been withdrawn, the heart is the abode or seat; [as it is said]: "Taking these particles of light (*tejomātrā*), he descends into the heart itself."

Thus says the Śruti. Furthermore, the departure [of the self] is heard of as being preceded by the blazing of the tip [of the heart] and having the eyes and other locations as its points of exit: "The tip of this very heart blazes forth; by that light, this Self departs—either through the eye, or through the crown of the head, or through other [parts of the body]."

"or from the parts of the body" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upani�sad 4.4.2). Regarding the doubt as to whether this [departure] occurs without any restriction for both the knower and the ignorant, or if there is some specific rule for the knower—since the scripture mentions no distinction, the state of non-restriction would initially follow—it is declared: for it is the same for both the knower and the ignorant.
When the heart is illumined at its tip and its door is thus revealed, the man of knowledge departs from the very place of the head, whereas others depart from other locations.
Why? Because of the power of their specific knowledge.
If even the wise man were to depart from just any part of the body like others, he would certainly not attain the superior world;
in that case, knowledge would be entirely purposeless.

Therefore, because of the connection with the recollection of the remaining path, one must practice the path prescribed in specific branches of knowledge—the path connected to the *nāḍī* at the crown of the head which constitutes a remainder of knowledge. By practicing that, he becomes firmly established in that very [world].

This is logical. Therefore, the wise person, favored by Brahman who dwells in the heart when well-worshipped, having attained its state, departs through the hundred-and-first channel— that which exceeds the hundred— while others depart through the other channels.
For thus, with reference to the knowledge of the heart, they recite: "There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head.
Going upwards by that, one attains immortality; the others lead in various directions for departing" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6). // 17 //
The Section on the Rays. Sūtra 18:
[The soul] follows the rays.
There is the knowledge of the heart: "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1).
Having begun thus, [the passage] is prescribed.

In that context, beginning with "Now, these channels of the heart" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.1), after describing in detail the connection between the channels and the rays, it is said: "Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5).
Thus it is said; and again it is stated: "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6).
Therefore, it is understood that departing through the artery that exceeds the hundred, one departs following the rays of light.

Now, when the doubt arises as to whether the soul's following of the rays belongs to one dying at any time—whether by day or by night—or whether it belongs only to one dying by day, we first maintain the proposition that the soul follows the rays without distinction, because the scripture mentions no such distinction. (18)
If it is argued that [the soul does not follow the rays] at night, we say no; for the connection [of the channels with the rays] persists as long as the body exists, and scripture demonstrates this.

[Objection: Since there is a connection between the channels and the rays during the day, one who dies by day would follow the rays, but for a deceased person at night, this would not occur because the connection between the channels and the rays has been severed. [Response: No.
Because the connection between the channels and the rays exists as long as the body exists;
for the contact between the vessels and the rays persists for as long as the body lasts.
And scripture demonstrates this point: "From that sun they spread out and enter into these channels; from these channels they spread out and enter into that sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.2).
Thus, even during the nights of the summer season, the persistence of the rays is perceived through the observation of effects such as heat;
however, because their persistence is slight, they are difficult to discern, as in the case of other seasonal nights or on cloudy days in the winter.
And the statement, "He places this very [light] in the night," demonstrates precisely this.
Moreover, if a deceased person were to ascend upwards at night even without following the rays, then the pursuit of the rays would be rendered useless.
For it is not specifically taught that "he who dies by day ascends upwards depending on the rays, whereas he who dies by night does so without depending on them.

Furthermore, if even a man of knowledge were not to ascend upwards merely due to the fault of dying at night, then knowledge would have only an occasional result, and there would consequently be no inclination toward its practice.
Because the time of death is not fixed;
furthermore, even if one has died at night, one would have to wait for the arrival of day.
And even upon the arrival of day, his body might—due to contact with fire or other elements—become unfit for connection with the rays [of the sun].
And the Śruti text, "As soon as he would turn his mind, so quickly he goes to the sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5), shows that there is no waiting for the initiation.
Therefore, this following of the rays occurs without distinction during both night and day. // 19 //
11. Section on the Southern Solstice (Dakṣiṇāyana-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 20–21.
"And therefore, also during the southern course.

(BBs 4.2.20) For this very reason—because waiting [for a specific time] is untenable, because the fruit of knowledge is not partial, and because death occurs at no fixed time—the wise man attains the fruit of knowledge even if he dies during the southern course.

This sūtra dispels the following doubt: "Since there is no established praise for dying during the northern course of the sun (uttarāyaṇa), and since we see Bhīṣma waiting [for it], and because of the Śruti text, 'From the bright fortnight, those six months during which the sun moves northward' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5), the northern course must be awaited. [The sūtra replies:
The established praise for the northern course refers only to those who lack knowledge.
The waiting upon Bhīṣma was for the purpose of observing proper conduct and for the purpose of demonstrating that he possessed the power of death at his own will, obtained through his father's grace.
As for the meaning of the Śruti, the author will state it later: "But [the deities] are conducting [souls], because of the mark thereof" (Brahmasūtra 4.3.4). // 20 //

But surely, having begun with the primacy of time in the statement: "I shall declare that time at which departing yogins go either to non-return or to return, O bull of the Bharatas" (Gītā 8.23), and having prescribed specific times such as the day for the sake of non-return in the Smṛti, how could one who departs during the night or during the southern solstice attain non-return?
To this it is replied:
"And these two are remembered for yogins, and they are of the nature of recollection" (BBs 4.2.21).
And this application of time, beginning with the day, is remembered for yogins as leading to non-return.
Moreover, these two—Yoga and Sāṃkhya—are Smārta (based on Smṛti), not Śrauta (based on Śruti).
Therefore, due to the difference in subject matter and the lack of a specific scriptural authority, this Smārta application of time does not apply to the Śrauta forms of knowledge.
Now, [one might object]: "Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice..."

And by the words, "Smoke, night, likewise the dark fortnight, and the six months of the southern solstice" (Gītā 8.24–25), these two paths—the path of the gods and the path of the ancestors—are recognized as being mentioned in the Smṛti just as they are in the Śruti.
To this it is replied: "I shall describe that time" (Gītā 8.23).
Thus, having raised the objection of contradiction because the Smṛti mentions "time," a resolution has been stated.
However, when even in the Smṛti the deities such as Agni and others are understood to be the conducting deities (ativāhikyaḥ), then there is no contradiction whatsoever. // 21 //
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the illustrious Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
The Third Quarter of the Fourth Chapter.
In this quarter, the northern path for one who possesses knowledge of the qualified Brahman (saguṇavidyā) after death is described.
Section 1: The Topic of the Path Beginning with Light (Arcirādi-adhikaraṇa).
Sūtra 1: [The soul proceeds] by way of light and so forth, because that is well-known.
It has been stated that the departure is the same for all until the commencement of the journey.
The path, however, is heard of in various ways in different Vedic texts.
In one way, it is described through the connection of the channels and the rays: "Then he ascends upwards by these very rays" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5).
In another way, it begins with light: "They reach the light, from the light to the day" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15).

Another [text] says: "Having reached this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.3). Another says: "When a person departs from this world, he comes to Vāyu" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.10.1). And another says:
"Free from passion, they depart through the gate of the sun" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.11).
And thus there is another [passage].
Regarding this, a doubt arises: are these paths mutually distinct, or is it rather one single path with multiple qualifications?
On this point, the initial position is that these paths are indeed distinct.

Because they belong to different contexts, and because they are distinct insofar as they are subordinate to different meditations (*upāsanā*). Furthermore: "Now, by these very rays... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5).

Thus, the restriction [implied by "only"] would be contradicted if there were dependence on the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), and the statement regarding speed— "As quickly as one could cast the mind, so far he goes to the sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5)— would also be strained. Therefore, these paths are indeed distinct from one another.

This being the case, we reply: "By the way beginning with light. We maintain that every seeker of Brahman proceeds by the very path beginning with light. Why? Because of its renown; for this path is well-known to all the wise.

For instance, in the section concerning the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), the scripture declares that even those who practice another form of knowledge— namely, "those who, in the forest, worship faith as truth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15)—
follow the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*). This might be so.

Regarding those Vidyās in which no specific path is mentioned, let this path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) apply; but as for those in which another path is heard, why should the path beginning with light be adopted?
To this it is replied: This would indeed be so if these paths were absolutely distinct.

However, we maintain that there is only one single path leading to the world of Brahman (brahmaloka), which possesses many attributes and is characterized in various places by various specific attributes.
Because there is recognition of a single part everywhere, the relationship of mutual qualifier and qualified is established.

For even when there is a difference in context, if the knowledge (*vidyā*) is one, there occurs the inclusion of mutual qualifiers, just as there is an inclusion of the specific details of the path. However, even when the knowledge differs, because there is recognition of a single part of the path and because the goal to be reached is non-different, the path itself is indeed non-different.

For thus it is said: "In those worlds of Brahman they dwell as supreme beings, far beyond" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15); "In that [world] they dwell for eternal years" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.10.1);
and "Whatever victory and whatever splendor belong to Brahman, that victory he wins and that splendor he attains" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.4).

Furthermore, in various places it is shown that this very same single fruit—characterized by the attainment of the world of Brahman—is the result, as in the passage: "Those who find this world of Brahman through celibacy" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.3).
As for the restriction "only by these," it would not apply if one were to rely on the path beginning with light (arcirādi).
This is not a fault,
because this [passage] has the reaching of the rays as its primary purpose.
For a single word cannot both cause one to reach the rays and exclude the *arciḥ* (flame) and so forth.
Therefore, it should be understood that this refers specifically to the connection with the rays.

As for the mention of speed, even when there is dependence on the path beginning with light (*arcis*), it is not contradicted because its purpose is to indicate swiftness in relation to other destinations, as in the expression:
"one arrives here in the mere twinkling of an eye."

Moreover, by stating that for those who have fallen away from either of these two paths there is a "terrible third place" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.8), the text proclaims a single Devayāna path— distinct from the Pitṛyāṇa and characterized by stages such as light (arcis)— as the one true way. Furthermore,
the stages of the path in the sequence beginning with light are numerous, whereas elsewhere they are few.

Furthermore, it is logical that the few should be led in accordance with the majority; for this reason also, it was stated [in the Sūtra] that "that [attainment of Brahman] is well-known by way of the path beginning with light" (arcir-ādi). // 1 //
2. Section on Vāyu. Sūtra 2:
"Vāyu [is reached] after the year, because of both non-distinction and distinction.

(BBs 4.3.2) But by what specific arrangement of sequence do these various stages of movement stand in a relationship of mutual qualifier and qualified? Being a friend to his students, the Teacher weaves this out for them.

"Having entered this path of the gods, he comes to the world of fire (agniloka), then to the world of wind, then to the world of Indra, then to the world of Prajāpati, and then to the world of Brahman" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.3).
Thus is the path of the gods recited by the Kauṣītakins.
In this context, since the words *arcis* and *agniloka* both denote the blazing [fire], they have a single meaning; therefore, no particular order of succession need be sought here.

But it has not been stated that Vāyu exists on the path beginning with light; in what place, then, is he to be inserted? It is said: "They go to the light itself; from the light to the day; from the day to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight to those six months when the sun moves northward; from the months to the year; from the year to the sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1, 2).
Thus, in this context, they reach Vāyu, who is beyond the year and yet below Āditya.
Why?
Because of both the general and the specific.

For instance, while the wind mentioned here in the passage "He [goes] to the world of Vāyu" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.3) is taught without qualification, a specific qualification of that same wind is seen in another Śruti:
"When a person departs from this world, he goes to the wind; there the wind makes way for him, as the hole of a chariot wheel."
"By that [path], he ascends upwards; he reaches the sun" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.10.1).
Because of this specific distinction—the observation that Vāyu precedes Āditya—Vāyu must be placed in the interval between the year (Abda) and Āditya.
But why, on account of the specific distinction of observing that [Vāyu] follows Agni, is Vāyu not placed immediately after Arcis?
We say that there is no such distinction here.
But has not the Śruti been cited: "Having reached this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni, then to the world of Vāyu, then to the world of Varuṇa" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.3)?
It is replied: In this case, there is merely a sequential arrangement of the text; there is no statement regarding a temporal sequence of travel.
There is a certain word;

for here only the indication of the meaning of the terms is performed, namely, "he comes to this and that. But in the other [passage], the sequence is understood: "having ascended upwards through a hole the size of a chariot wheel provided by the wind, he reaches the sun."
Therefore, it is well said: "by means of the non-specific and the specific.
However, the Vājasaneyins record: "From the months to the world of the gods, from the world of the gods to the sun" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15).
In that regard, after reaching the Ādityas by way of the intermediate sacrifice, they would pass into the world of the gods and then into Vāyu;
however, the statement "from Vāyu into the year" is made with reference to the Chāndogya Śruti.
For in the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka, the world of the gods is absent in one place, while the year is absent in the other.
In that regard, because of the evidence of two scriptural passages, both [the year and the world of the gods] are to be connected with both [the moon and the sun].
Even there, one must distinguish that the year comes first and the world of the gods comes later, due to their connection with the month. // 2 //
3. The Section Concerning Lightning. Sūtra 3:
Varuṇa [is reached] after lightning, because of the connection. Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5: "From the sun to the moon, from the moon to lightning."
Thus, above this lightning, "that world of Varuṇa"—this Varuṇa is connected [to it].
For there is indeed a connection between lightning and Varuṇa;
for when the vast lightnings, with their intense thundering sounds, dance within the bellies of the clouds, then the waters fall down.
And there is a Brāhmaṇa passage stating, "It lightens, it thunders, or it will rain" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.11.1).
Furthermore, it is well known from both Śruti and Smṛti that Varuṇa is the lord of the waters.

Indra and Prajāpati [follow] Varuṇa, because there is no other place for them and by virtue of the force of the textual sequence. Furthermore, because they are not mentioned in the list of intermediate stages, Varuṇa and the others are placed at the very end, as there is no specific location for them; and lightning is included at the end in the path beginning with light (*arcis*). // 3 //
4. The Section on the Conveying Deities (Ātivāhika Adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 4–6.
"The conveying deities [are those mentioned], because of their characteristic mark" (BBs 4.3.4).
Regarding these very [stages] beginning with light, there is a doubt: are these signs of the path, or places of enjoyment, or rather leaders of the travelers?
In this regard, it is first established that the light (*arcis*) and so forth constitute the characteristics of the path, because the instruction consists in their essential nature.
For just as in the world, someone intending to set out for a village or a city is instructed: "Go, you..."
"Just as one might say, 'From here you will reach that mountain, then the banyan tree, then the river, then the village,
or then the city,' so too here [the Buddha] says, 'The rays [go] from day to the waxing fortnight,' and so forth;
or rather, it is understood that these are the planes of enjoyment."
For instance, [the text] connects the word "world" (*loka*) with Agni and others, as in: "He goes to the world of Agni" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.3), and so forth.
Furthermore, the word "world" is used to denote the abodes of enjoyment for living beings, as in: "The world of men, the world of the fathers, the world of the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16).
Likewise, the Brāhmaṇa states: "They become attached to those worlds, which are days and nights," and so on.
Therefore, the light and the other stages are not conductors.
Furthermore, their status as conductors is untenable because they are insentient;
for in the world, it is sentient persons appointed by a king who conduct those to be conducted along difficult paths.
This being the case, we reply: these [beings] must indeed be *ātivāhika* (conveying spirits).
Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of that; for it is said: "From the moon to lightning, there a person who is not human—he leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5).
Thus, he demonstrates that the capacity to cause [the object] to be known is established.
If it is argued that "that statement is exhausted merely with respect to its own subject," we say no;
for the qualification has as its purpose the exclusion of the state of being a mere human being (mānavatva).

If it is argued that the persons who lead [the soul] through the path beginning with light (arcis) are understood to be human beings (mānava), then it is appropriate to apply the qualification "non-human" (amānava) to those persons in order to exclude them. // 4 //
[Objection: But surely that mere mark (liṅga) is not a means of cognition because of the absence of a logical rule (nyāya).
[Response: This is not a fault, because its establishment results from the delusion of both parties.
Since those paths beginning with light (*arcis*) involve the collection of the group of organs upon separation from the body, they are not independent;

and since the light and so forth are themselves insentient, they lack independence. Therefore, it is understood that specific conscious deities presiding over the light and so forth are appointed for the journey beyond.
For even in the world, those who are intoxicated, unconscious, and so forth, have their faculties constricted and proceed along paths directed by others.
Furthermore, because the light and other stages are not constant, it is not logical for them to constitute the characteristics of a path;
for it is not possible for a deceased person at night to encounter the nature of the day.
And it has been stated previously that there is no [need for] guarding;
however, because the deities are eternal, this fault does not apply to them.

Furthermore, their designation by terms such as "light" (*arcis*) and so forth is appropriate because they are the presiding deities (*abhimānin*) over light and the rest, as in: "From light to day" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5).
This and other such instructions are not contradicted even by the fact that [the beings] are *ativāhika* (conveying); for by means of the light as the cause, one reaches the day;
and by means of the day as the cause, one reaches the waxing fortnight.
Likewise, even among those well-known in the world who are *ativāhika*, such a type of instruction is observed.
"Go from here to Balavarman, then to Jayasiṃha, and then to Kṛṣṇagupta. Moreover, in the opening passage, "They reach the light" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15),
only a general connection is stated, not any specific kind of connection.

In the conclusion, however, the specific relationship characterized as being a "conductor" (*ativāhika*)—expressed in the words, "He leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.6)—is stated; by this, it is determined that he is the same person referred to at the beginning as well. Furthermore, because their organs are withdrawn into a state of integration (*saṃpiṇḍita-karaṇatva*), no experience of enjoyment is possible for those travelers there.

However, the word "world" (*loka*) can be applied even to those who do not themselves experience [the results], because it serves as the ground of enjoyment for others dwelling there. Therefore, it should be understood that one who has reached the world presided over by Agni is conducted across by Agni, and one who has reached the world presided over by Vāyu is conducted across by Vāyu. // 5 //
But how, on the view that [the path] is one of conveyance (*ativāhika*), can that [conveying] be possible in the case of Varuṇa and the others?

For Varuṇa and the rest are introduced as being "beyond lightning," yet it is heard in scripture that immediately after lightning, until the attainment of Brahman, the agency of conveying belongs exclusively to the non-human person (*amānava*). To this, he recites the following answer:
"Because of that hearing [from scripture] immediately after the lightning.

(BBs 4.3.6) Therefore, it must be understood that after reaching the lightning, those being conducted by the non-human person (amānava-puruṣa) through the worlds of Varuṇa and others—proceeding immediately after the lightning—go to the world of Brahman.
This is because of the scriptural statement regarding his role as the conductor: "The non-human person, coming from the lightning, leads them to the world of Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5).
However, Varuṇa and the others should be understood as being benefactors of that very [soul] by means of some form of assistance, either by not creating obstacles or by performing supportive actions.
Therefore, it is rightly said that the deities beginning with Light (arcis) are the conducting selves (ativāhika). // 6 //

5. The Section Concerning the Effect (Kāryādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 7–14. Sūtra 7: Bādari [holds that the soul goes] to the effected Brahman, because the journey is possible for it. "He leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5).
Thus, a doubt arises here: does [the path] lead to the effected (kārya) Brahman, or rather to the supreme, unmodified, primary Brahman?
Whence this doubt?
From the use of the word "Brahman" and from the scriptural mention of "going."

In this regard, the teacher Bādari maintains that it is the effected Brahman itself—the lower Brahman endowed with qualities—that leads these [souls], by means of a non-human person (*amānavaḥ puruṣaḥ*). Why? Because the journey to it is logically possible;
for it is indeed logical that this effected Brahman is the destination to be reached.
For it is appropriate that this effected Brahman (kāryabrahman) is to be reached, because it possesses spatial extension;

however, in the case of the supreme Brahman, neither the state of being a goer, nor the state of being a destination, nor the act of going is possible, because [the supreme Brahman] is omnipresent and is the inner self of the goers themselves. // 7 //
And because of being specified:

from another scriptural passage, "He leads them to the worlds of Brahman; they dwell in those highest worlds of Brahman, in the highest of the high" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15), it is understood that the journey has as its object only the effected (kārya) Brahman, since it is thus specifically distinguished.
For a plural qualification is not possible in the case of the supreme Brahman;

however, in the case of the effect, a plural number is possible because a distinction of states is logically consistent. Furthermore, common worldly usage and scriptural tradition apply directly only to that which pertains to transformation—that is, to a place of experience characterized by a specific arrangement.
But elsewhere, in passages such as "This world, O Emperor, is indeed Brahman," the term is used in a secondary (gauṇī) sense.

Furthermore, even the designation of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and that which is to be located therein (*adhikartavya*) would not be directly applicable to the supreme Brahman. Therefore, this leading [of the soul] has as its object only the effected (kārya) Brahman. // 8 //

But surely, even with respect to the effect, the word "Brahman" is not appropriate, for it has been established in the section on Concordance (*samanvaya*) that [Brahman] is the cause of the origin and so forth of the entire world.
To this it is replied: "But that designation [of the effect] is due to proximity" (BS 1.4.3).
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of removing a doubt.
Because of its proximity to the Supreme Brahman, the application of the term "Brahman" to the lower Brahman is not contradictory even in that case.

For it is an established principle that the Supreme Brahman itself, when connected with pure limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and taught for the sake of meditation through certain modified attributes such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth, is designated as the "lower" Brahman.
But surely, if the goal were merely an effect, the scriptural teaching of non-return would not be tenable;
for they do not conceive of eternal existence anywhere other than in the supreme Brahman. Moreover, scripture demonstrates that those who have set out on the path of the gods do not return.

If it is argued that there is no return for them here, as stated in "Those proceeding by this path do not return to this human whirlpool" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.6), and "Going upwards from those two, one attains immortality" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6; Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.16),
we reply as follows:
"Because of the statement that [they go] from here with their presider when the dissolution of the effect has occurred.

(BBs 4.3.10) When the dissolution of the world of the effected Brahman is imminent, those who have produced right vision (*samyagdarśana*) right there, together with Hiraṇyagarbha— the presider over that world— proceed from here to the supreme, perfectly pure state of Viṣṇu.
Gradual liberation must be accepted on the basis of scriptural declarations such as "not returning" and so forth;
for it has been established that the attainment of the Supreme cannot possibly occur directly without being preceded by a journey. // 10 //
And because of Smṛti:
Smṛti also confirms this point: "When the dissolution has arrived, at the end of the supreme [Brahmā], all those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state together with Brahmā."
Therefore, the established conclusion is that the scriptural teaching regarding the journey has as its object the effected Brahman (kāryabrahma). // 11 //

But what is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that was anticipated, in response to which this established conclusion (*siddhānta*) was set forth by [the Sūtras] beginning with "Bādari [holds that the soul goes] for the sake of the task" (BS 4.3.7)?
That is now demonstrated by the Sūtras themselves:
"But Jaimini [holds it to be] the Supreme, because of its being the primary meaning.
The teacher Jaimini, however, maintains that in the passage "He leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.6), it is the Supreme Brahman itself that he leads them to.
Why? Because of its primacy;
for the Supreme Brahman is the primary referent of the word "Brahman," while the lower [Brahman] is secondary.
And when there is a connection between the primary and the secondary, the cognition occurs with respect to the primary. // 12 //
And because of the scriptural vision:
"Going upwards by that, one attains immortality" (Chāndogya 8.6.6; Kaṭha 6.16), which shows that immortality is preceded by a journey.
And immortality is possible only in the supreme Brahman, not in the effected [Brahman], because the effected is perishable;
for it is said: "But where one sees something else, that is the finite, that is mortal" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).

Thus it is stated in the scripture; moreover, this very path is taught in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad as having the Supreme as its sole object, for there is no introduction to any other knowledge therein, as seen in the passage: "Other than dharma, other than adharma" (Ka. 2.14).
Thus, because it is the Supreme Brahman alone that has been introduced as the subject. // 13 //
Nor is there an intention to attain the effected [Brahman].

Furthermore, the intention to attain expressed in the passage, "I enter the hall and the dwelling of Prajāpati" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1), does not have the effected [Brahman] as its object; for it continues, "That which is the sustainer of name and form, and that which is within them—that is Brahman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1)
This is because the Supreme Brahman, which is distinct from its effects, is the subject under discussion;
furthermore, it is introduced as the Self of all in the passage, "I become the glory of the Brāhmaṇas" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1).
And because it is well known that the supreme Brahman alone possesses fame and name, as stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (4.19): "There is no likeness of Him whose name is great glory."

Furthermore, this attainment of the abode is preceded by a journey, as stated in the context of the knowledge of the Heart: "That is the unconquered city of Brahman, the golden hall built by the Lord" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.5.3).
Since the root *pad* also has the meaning of "going," it is determined that a path is required.
Therefore, there is another position: that the scriptural texts concerning "going" have the Supreme Brahman as their object.
These two positions were formulated by the Teacher: one based on the [modes of] rebirth, birth, and so forth, and the other based on primacy and so forth.

In this regard, the modes of rebirth, birth, and so forth are capable of making primacy and the rest appear as such, but primacy and the rest cannot make the modes of rebirth, birth, and so forth appear as such; thus, the first alone is explained as the established tenet, while the second is not.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:
There is no one who issues a command that the primary meaning alone must be accepted even when [another] possibility exists.

Furthermore, even in the context of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), the mention of the path belonging to another form of knowledge for the purpose of praise is appropriate, just as in the passage: "The others go upward in various directions at the time of departure" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6).

However, by breaking off the preceding sentence, the intention to attain even the effected [Brahman] in the passage "I enter the assembly hall and the residence of Prajāpati" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1) is not contradicted.

Furthermore, even with respect to Brahman endowed with qualities, the proclamation of its being the self of all— as in "possessing all works, possessing all desires," and so forth— is entirely appropriate.
Therefore, the scriptural texts concerning the departure [of the soul] refer exclusively to the Supreme [Brahman].

However, some, adhering to the established rule that the preceding sūtras constitute prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the subsequent ones constitute the final conclusions (*siddhānta*), maintain that these texts on departure refer to something other than the Supreme; that is untenable.
Because it is impossible for Brahman to be something that must be gone to;

for the supreme Brahman is all-pervading, internal to all, and the self of all, as stated in: "It is omnipresent and eternal like space" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1), "That Brahman which is immediate and direct" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1), and "The Self which is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1).

Since its specific nature has been determined by such scriptural passages as "All this is indeed the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2) and "Brahman alone is all this, the most excellent" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11), it is never logically possible for that [Self] to be an object to be reached.
For that which has already been traversed is not being traversed;

indeed, it is well known in the world that one thing goes to another. [Objection: But is it not observed in the world that even what has been traversed is to be traversed again when distinguished by another location?

Just as one who remains on the earth itself goes to another place by means of the earth, so too, even though there is non-difference [between the self and Brahman], because Brahman is endowed with all powers, there might somehow be the state of being an object to be gone to. No;
for all specific distinctions have been denied of Brahman.
"Partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19);
"Neither gross, nor subtle, nor short, nor long" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8);
"For it is unborn, both within and without" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).
"Verily, this great unborn Self is undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25);
"This Self is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26)—
from such scriptural passages, traditional texts, and logical reasoning, it is impossible to conceive of any association with distinctions such as space or time in the Supreme Self.
By which [means] there would be a state of being "to-be-gone-to" for this [Brahman] according to the logic of location and temporal state;
however, since location and time possess specific distinctions such as place and state, it is possible for there to be a "state of being to-be-gone-to" qualified by space and time.
If it is argued that Brahman possesses manifold powers because of the scriptural revelation that it is the cause of the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world, we say: no.
If it is argued that the scriptures negating distinctions have no other purpose [than to establish non-duality],
and that the same applies to the scriptures concerning origination and so forth— [we reply: No,
for those [latter] are intent upon establishing oneness.

Indeed, by means of examples such as clay and the like, the scripture—which establishes the reality of the one existent Brahman and the illusory nature of its modifications—cannot have as its primary purpose the origination and so forth [of the world].
Why, then, is it that the scriptures concerning origination and so forth are subordinate to the others, rather than the others being subordinate to them?
It is said: because the scriptures that negate specific distinctions possess a meaning that leaves no further expectancy for further qualification.

For when the oneness, eternality, purity, and so forth of the Self have been realized, no further desire arises, because the understanding that the human goal has been accomplished is established. As it is said: "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? (Īśā Upaniṣad 7);
and "Truly, O Janaka, you have attained fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4).

"From nothing does the knower fear; indeed, this [realization] does not afflict him: 'Why have I not done what is good? Why have I committed evil? (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9.1), and so forth, according to such scriptural passages.
Likewise, because we observe that the wise experience contentment, bliss,

and so forth, and because there is a censure of the false notion of modification in the passage, "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity," it cannot be understood that the scriptural texts negating distinctions are subsidiary to anything else.
The scriptural passages concerning origination and so forth do not possess the capacity to convey a meaning that leaves no further expectancy;
rather, their purpose as something else is clearly perceived.
For instance: "In this regard, my dear, understand this sprout that has emerged; it cannot be without a root" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.3).
Having thus introduced the subject, he shows at the conclusion that only the one existent root of the universe is to be known:
"That from which indeed these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter when they pass away."
And also: "Seek to know that;
that is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1).
Thus, since the scriptural texts concerning origination and so forth have as their ultimate purpose the realization of the oneness of the Self, Brahman does not possess multiple powers.
And for this reason, the state of being an object of going is untenable;
furthermore, the text "His vital breaths do not depart; being Brahman, he merges into Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6) precludes any movement toward the supreme Brahman.
That has been explained under the sūtra, "For [the path] is clear to some" (Brahma-sūtra 4.2.13).
Furthermore, if one were to conceive of a movement, the individual soul (*jīva*) as the mover would have to be either a part or a modification of Brahman, the goal to be reached;
for if there were absolute identity, movement would be impossible.
If that were so, what would follow? It is said:
if it were a single part, then because that part is eternally connected with the possessor of the parts (*ekadeśin*), the further proceeding toward Brahman would not be possible.
Furthermore, the conception of Brahman as having parts is untenable, because it is well-established that Brahman is partless (*niravayava*).
Even on the view that it is subject to modification (*vikāra*), this objection remains equal; for the modified object is eternally connected with its modifier.
Indeed, a jar does not exist while abandoning its nature as clay; if it were to abandon it, it would result in non-existence.

Furthermore, whether [the soul] be considered a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*) [of Brahman], its transition into the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is untenable, because Brahman— the possessor of those qualities— is eternal. Alternatively, if the individual soul (*jīva*) were indeed distinct from Brahman,
it would have to be either atomic (*aṇu*), all-pervading (*vyāpin*), or of intermediate size (*madhyama-parimāṇa*).
If it were all-pervading, movement would be impossible;
if it were of intermediate size, there would be the consequence of impermanence;
and if it were minute, the sensation of the entire body would be impossible.
Furthermore, the atomicity and intermediate size [of the soul] have already been refuted in detail previously;
moreover, if the individual soul were different from the Supreme, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).

This same defect applies equally to the positions that [the whole] is either a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*). If it is argued that there is no fault because the modification and the part are non-different from their possessors (*tadvat*), we say no; for primary oneness (*mukhyam ekatvam*) is untenable.
In all these positions, there follows the consequence of no liberation,
because the transmigrating nature of the self has not ceased;
or, if it were to cease, there would follow the consequence of the destruction of its own essential nature.
And because the identity of Brahman and the Self is not accepted [by them].
As for what is prattled by some: "Eternal and occasional rites are performed so that no transgression arises;
optional and prohibited rites are avoided so as not to incur heaven or hell; and those [fruits] to be experienced in the present body [are exhausted]."

And since karmas are exhausted solely through experience, there will be no cause for the reconnection with another body after the fall of the present body; thus, even without liberation characterized by abiding in one's own true nature, liberation will be achieved for one who lives in this manner simply by virtue of being the Self of Brahman.
That is incorrect.
Because there is a lack of authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For this has not been established by any scripture that one seeking liberation should act in such a manner.
Rather, this is merely conjectured by one's own fancy: "Since saṃsāra is caused by karma, it will cease to exist due to the absence of its cause."
And this cannot even be conjectured, because the absence of causal signs is difficult to discern.
For it is possible that many karmas accumulated over various lifetimes, which have desirable and undesirable ripenings, belong to each individual being;
since it is impossible for those actions with contradictory results to be experienced simultaneously, some of them remain waiting for their opportunity—this [is the case].

However, since some births are produced that await specific place, time, and cause, and because it is impossible to exhaust those remaining [karmas] through present experience alone, it cannot be determined with certainty that even for one whose conduct has been described as above, there will be an absence of causes for another body upon the fall of the current body.
Furthermore, the existence of residual karma (*karmaśe�ṣa*) is established by such scriptural and traditional texts as, "Those here whose conduct was pleasant, by that remainder...
It might be argued that the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites will serve as the expiators of those [residuals].
That is not so, because there is no contradiction;
for it is only when a contradiction exists that the relationship between the sublated and the sublator occurs.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the meritorious deeds accumulated in other births and the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, because they are indistinguishable in their pure nature. However, since evil deeds (*durita*) consist of impurity, there may indeed be a destruction of them when a contradiction arises; yet, by that much alone, the non-existence of the cause for another body is not established.
This is because it is logical that [the cessation of suffering] is caused by well-performed deeds (*sukṛta*).
Furthermore, there is no understanding of the complete exhaustion even of misconduct (*duścarita*).

Nor is there any authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that the mere non-occurrence of demerit (*pratyavāya*) results from the performance of obligatory and occasional rites, rather than the production of another fruit; for it is possible that another fruit may also arise as a concomitant result.

For Āpastamba indeed records: "Just as when a mango tree is intended for its fruit, shade and fragrance arise as secondary effects, so too when one practices Dharma, worldly benefits arise as secondary effects.

And it is not possible for anyone to promise, from birth until death, the total avoidance of optional and prohibited acts in the absence of right vision (samyak-darśana), for even those who are most skillful are seen to commit subtle transgressions.
Even if it were to be doubted, the non-existence of such a sign remains difficult to ascertain.

Furthermore, if the identity of Brahman and the Self—which is accessible through knowledge—is not accepted, it is impossible to desire isolation (*kaivalya*) for a Self whose very nature consists of agency and enjoyership;
for that which is inherent in one's nature, like the heat of fire, cannot be avoided.

It might be argued as follows: "The state of being an agent and the state of being an enjoyer are the effect (kārya), which is an undesirable thing (anartha), not the capacity (śakti). Therefore, even while the capacity remains, liberation is logically established through the cessation of the effect.
But that is not so.
For when a capacity exists, the production of its effect is unavoidable.
Now, it might be argued that a capacity does not initiate an effect on its own without depending on other causal conditions;
therefore, even though it remains solitary, it is not at fault.
But that is not so;
for even the marks (nimitta) are eternally connected by way of a relationship characterized by potency (śakti).

Therefore, as long as the nature of being an agent and an enjoyer exists, there can be no hope whatsoever for liberation, even if there were another reality consisting of the identity with Brahman accessible through knowledge.
And scripture states: "There is no other path for going" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8), which excludes any path to liberation other than knowledge.
Furthermore, even though the individual soul is non-different from the Supreme, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of all worldly activity.
If it is argued that this is because means of valid cognition such as perception do not operate [in that state], we say no;
for it is possible [to speak of them] prior to awakening, just like the conventional usage of dreams.
And the scripture says: "For where there is, as it were, duality, there one sees another" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14, 4.5.15).

Having thus described the empirical operation of perception and other means of knowledge regarding the sphere of the unawakened, [the scripture] again demonstrates their absence in the sphere of the awakened through such passages as, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).
Therefore, since for the knower of the Supreme Brahman the cognition of a destination and so forth is sublated, a journey of any kind cannot possibly be established.
But what is the subject matter of these scriptural passages concerning the path?
It is said: they will have as their subject matter knowledge with attributes (*saguṇavidyā*).

For instance, in some places, the path is described in connection with the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), as in: "Breath is Brahman; Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10.5).

Thus, regarding the passage, "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1), even there, because the qualified [Brahman] alone is to be meditated upon through qualities such as being the "leader of the path" (*vāmanī*) and so forth, as well as having "true desires" (*satyakāma*) and so forth, the going is possible.
Nowhere is a going concerning the supreme Brahman heard of, just as the prohibition of going is heard: "His vital breaths do not depart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).

In passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), although the root *āp* has the sense of "going," this [attainment] is designated as the realization of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-pratipatti*), because reaching another location is impossible according to the reasoning already described; it is stated with reference to the dissolution of name and form superimposed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
This should be understood as being like [the statement] "Being Brahman, he attains Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7) and so forth.
Moreover, if the journey were explained as having the Supreme as its object, it would be either for the sake of encouragement or for the sake of contemplation.
In this regard, the inducement is first accomplished by means of the statement that there is no [further] journey for the knower of Brahman;
for that [state] is established through the very health bestowed by knowledge, which is self-evident and immediate.

Furthermore, no requirement whatsoever can be established for reflecting upon the destiny of that knowledge which reveals eternally accomplished liberation and possesses a fruit that is not to be achieved.
Therefore, the "going" (gati) refers to the lower Brahman.

In this context, due to a failure to discern between the higher and the lower Brahman, the scriptural passages concerning the going that apply to the lower Brahman are superimposed upon the higher Brahman.
"Are there two Brahmans, the higher and the lower?
"Certainly, there are two; for it is seen [in scripture] that 'O Satyakāma, this syllable Om is indeed the higher and the lower Brahman'" (Praśna Upaniṣad 5.2), and so forth.
What, then, is the higher Brahman and what is the lower?
It is said:

that Brahman which is taught by means of words such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) and so forth, through the negation of specific distinctions such as name and form created by ignorance (*avidyā*), is the higher.

That very same [Brahman] is the lower when it is taught for the purpose of meditation as qualified by some particularity such as name and form, through such words as "consisting of mind, having breath for its body, whose form is light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2).
But would this not contradict the scripture concerning non-duality? No.
Because [the Self] is freed from the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of name and form created by ignorance (*avidyā*),

the fruit of that meditation on the lower Brahman— which is heard in its proximity as "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1), etc.— is indeed the sphere of transmigratory existence, characterized by sovereignty over the world.
Because ignorance has not been dispelled,
and because that [ignorance] is bound to a particular location, it is not contradictory for there to be movement toward reaching it.

Furthermore, even though the Self is all-pervading like space, we have already stated in the sūtra *tadguṇasāratvāt* (Brahmasūtra 2.3.29) that "movement" is conventionally established in reference to the movement of adjuncts such as the intellect, just as it is established when space enters into objects such as jars.
Thus it stands here;
therefore, this very position— that "Bādari [holds that the soul] is an effect" (Brahma-sūtra 4.3.7)— is the established view.
However, the sūtra "But Jaimini [holds] the opposite" (Brahma-sūtra 4.3.12) should be understood as merely presenting an alternative view for the purpose of expanding one's understanding. // 14 //
6. The Section on Non-Symbolic Meditations (Apratīkālam-banādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 15–16:
"Bādarāyaṇa holds that [the Lord] leads those who meditate on what is not a symbol, because there is a fault in both [other] cases, and because of the nature of their resolve" (BBs 4.3.15).
It has been established that the journey concerns the effect (the effected Brahman) and not the highest [Brahman].
Now this is being deliberated: does the non-human person lead all those who have undergone transformation, without distinction, to the world of Brahman, or only some of them?
What, then, is the prima facie position? It would seem that for all these knowers, there is a departure [to the world of Brahman] except for the case of the Supreme Brahman;
for it has been stated: "There is no restriction regarding all [the meditations]" (Brahma-sūtra 3.3.31).

Thus, since it has been stated here without distinction that these [souls] are introduced into other forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), this being the position reached, the author replies: "Except for those who have the *pratīka* as their support. The teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that, excluding those who have the *pratīka* as their support, all others who have the modified effects (*vikāra*) as their support are led to the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*).
For indeed, there is no fault whatsoever in accepting the non-existence [of the deity] in both ways,
since the principle of non-restriction applies even to meditations other than those involving a counter-form (*pratīka*).
And the nature of one's resolve (*kratu*) should be seen as the supporting cause for this twofold state;

for it is connected that he whose resolve is fixed on Brahman would attain the sovereignty of Brahman, according to the scriptural text: "In whatever way they meditate upon it, that very thing they become. However, in the case of symbols (*pratīka*), there is no resolve fixed on Brahman, because the meditation has the symbol as its primary object.
But is it not heard that even one whose sacrifice is not Brahman goes to Brahman, as in the Pañcāgnividyā: "He leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5)?

Let it be so where such an explicit statement is found; however, in its absence, by the general rule of "the nature of the sacrifice" (*tatkratu-nyāya*), it is understood that only those whose sacrifice is Brahman attain it, and not others—this is also shown by the scripture which points out a distinction. (Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya 4.3.16)

Regarding the meditations on the symbols (*pratīka*) such as Name and the rest, [the scripture] shows that for each successive meditation there is a specific excellence of fruit compared to the preceding one: "As far as Name extends, so far he has freedom of movement" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.5);
"Speech, indeed, is greater than Name" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.2.1).
"Or, as far as speech reaches, there he has freedom of movement as he desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.2.2), and "Mind, indeed, is greater than speech" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.3.1),
and so forth.
And this distinction of results is appropriate because meditations on symbols (*pratīka*) are dependent upon those symbols;
for if they were dependent upon Brahman, since Brahman is without distinction, how could there be a distinction of results?
Therefore, meditations that have symbols as their support do not possess the same results as the others. // 16 //
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govindabhagavatpūjyapāda.
Fourth Chapter, Fourth Quarter.
[In this quarter, there is an exposition of the attainment of Brahman and the state of existence in the world of Brahman.]
1. The Section on Manifestation upon Attainment (Saṃpadyāvirbhāvādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 1–3:
"Upon attaining [the Supreme], there is manifestation in its own form, because of the word 'own'.
(BBs 4.4.1) Thus it is heard in scripture: "In this very way, this serene being, having risen up from this body and having attained the highest light, manifests in its own form."
In this regard, there is a doubt: does [the self] arise through some adventitious distinction, as in the case of places of enjoyment such as the world of the gods, or rather by the self alone?
What, then, is the initial position? It should be that there is an arising through some adventitious form, just as in other locations.
Furthermore, liberation is well-known to be a fruit; and since "is accomplished" (*abhiniṣpadyate*) is a synonym for "arising," if this accomplishment were merely by way of its own nature,
it would have been manifest even in previous states, because its own nature does not depart [in those states].
Therefore, [the opponent claims] that it is manifested through some specific attribute.
This being the position reached, we reply: it manifests by means of the Self alone, and not through any other attribute.
Why? Because of the word "own" in the phrase "it is manifested in its own form."
Otherwise, the qualification "by its own word" would be inappropriate. [Objection:
But surely the word "own" (sva) will have the intended meaning of "belonging to oneself" (ātmīya). [Reply: No, because that [meaning] cannot be expressed [in this context].
For if it were established in any form whatsoever, then since that very form would logically belong to it as its own, the qualification "by itself" (*svena*) would be purposeless.
However, if it is taken to mean "by its own nature," it is meaningful; for it is established solely by its own essential nature (*ātmarūpa*), and not by any adventitious or extraneous form. // 1 //

But what is the distinction between the previous states and this one, given that they are equal in the sense that the essential nature does not perish? To this he says: "The liberated one, because of the declaration" (BBs 4.4.2). He who is said here to "attain" is released from all bonds and remains in his very pure self.
