In the previous [passage], however, there is this distinction: that the Self is described as being defiled by the three states, such that "he becomes blind," "as if he weeps," and "having gone to dissolution, he becomes as if non-existent.

But how is it understood that "this one is now liberated"? He says: "Because of the formal proposition. For instance: "I shall explain this very same thing to you further" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.3, 8.10.4, 8.11.3).

Thus, having proposed as the subject of exposition the Self which is free from the defects of the three states, and having introduced it with the words, "Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1), he concludes with the words, "He attains his own true nature; he is the Supreme Person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).
Likewise, even at the commencement of the narrative in the passage beginning with "That Self which is free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1), the proposition concerns only the liberated Self.
Furthermore, the well-known status of liberation as a fruit depends solely upon the cessation of bondage, not upon the production of something previously non-existent.

As for the statement that "he is accomplished," which is a synonym for arising, that too is in reference to a prior state, just as one says "he is accomplished as healthy" upon the cessation of a disease;
therefore, there is no fault. // 2 //
The Self [is meant], because of the context.
But how is it said that he is "liberated," when the text, "having reached the highest light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3), declares him to be within the very sphere of the effected [Brahman]?
Because the word *jyotis* (light) is conventionally established in the sense of elemental light,
and because no one who has not transcended the realm of modification can be liberated—
given that modification is well-known to be subject to suffering.
This is not a fault;

for by the word "light" (*jyotis*), the Supreme Self is indicated through the context, since it is the Supreme Self that is under discussion in the passage, "That Self which is free from evil, ageless, and deathless" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).
Indeed, it is not possible to suddenly take the light of the material elements to be meant here.
[Otherwise,] there would be the fallacy of abandoning the subject under discussion and introducing an irrelevant topic.

Furthermore, the word "light" (*jyotis*) is seen to refer even to the Self, as in the passage: "The gods [worship] that light which is beyond light" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.16). This has been explained at length in the commentary on *Brahma Sūtra* 1.3.40. // 3 //

Section 2: On Being Seen Without Separation. Sūtra 4: Because it is seen [in scripture] as being without separation. (BBs 4.4.4) Having attained the supreme light, he manifests in his own true form. Regarding the inquiry as to whether he exists as something distinct from the supreme Self or whether he remains without separation: [The opponent argues: He must exist as something distinct, because of the mention of "attaining" (*upasaṃpadya*). Just as when one attains a village or a city, one reaches a place different from oneself, so too, having attained the supreme light, he must become something different from that supreme Self. Furthermore, the mention of "manifesting in his own form" (*svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*) implies a distinction; for if he were not different, what need would there be for him to manifest? Moreover, the mention of "eating food" (*annam atti*) indicates a distinction, since one who eats food is different from the food itself. Also, the mention of "he moves about" (*sañcarati*) shows that he is different from the supreme Self, which is devoid of movement. Therefore, he exists as something distinct. [The author replies: This is not so. He remains without separation from the supreme Self. Why? Because it is seen [in scripture] as being without separation. For after stating, "Having attained the supreme light, he manifests in his own form," the text subsequently says, "He is that supreme, undecaying Being, which is seen as different from this body, consisting of the intellect, upward-leading, and beyond darkness" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3). Since he is described as being seen within that very same supreme Self, we understand that he remains without separation. Furthermore, the mention of "attaining" is used in the sense of reaching a state of non-separation, just as one might say, "He has attained the state of Brahman" (*brahmabhūta*), meaning he has become one with Brahman. As for the mention of "manifesting in his own form," that refers to the removal of the veil of ignorance; it does not imply a difference in essence. The mention of "eating food" is also figurative, referring to the enjoyment of the bliss of Brahman. And the mention of "moving about" refers to his capacity to assume various forms at will, not to physical locomotion. Therefore, he remains without separation from the supreme Self.

To one who holds the view that the liberated soul remains in a state of distinction— based on the indication of the locus and the object to be reached in the phrase "he moves about there" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3), and the indication of the agent and the object in the phrase "having attained the Light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3)— the author explains that the liberated soul remains as non-distinct from the Supreme Self.
Why? Because it is seen [in scripture]. For instance: "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7); "I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).

Passages such as "where one sees nothing else" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1) and "but there is no second thing, distinct from that, which he might see" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23), demonstrate the Supreme Self precisely through non-differentiation.
And it is logical that the fruit corresponds exactly to one's vision, according to the principle of "as is one's intention" (*tatkratu*):
"As pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like that, so, O Gautama, does the self of the sage who knows become. (KaU 4.15)
Thus, these and similar statements intended to define the nature of the liberated soul demonstrate non-differentiation alone;
so too do the illustrations of the river and the ocean.
As for the mention of difference, it is employed figuratively despite the absence of actual distinction.

For we see such scriptural passages as: "In what, O Venerable Sir, is He established? In His own majesty" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1), and "He who rejoices in the Self, who plays with the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2). // 4 //
3. The Section Concerning the Brahman (Brāhmādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 5–7.
Jaimini [holds that the soul departs] with its own [form], on account of the introductory statement and so forth.
It has been established that [the soul departs] "with its own form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4).

Thus, in this context, it is established that one manifests in the form of the Self alone, and not in some adventitious, other form. Now, however, in response to the desire to know its specific characteristics, it is stated: "His own nature is the state of Brahman, beginning with freedom from evil and ending with the power of true resolve; likewise, it consists of omniscience and omnipotence. It is in that very nature that one manifests.
Thus the teacher Jaimini thinks. Why? Because its being so is understood from the introductory statements and so forth. For instance:
"That Self which is free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).
By this introductory exposition ending with "whose desires are true, whose resolve is true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1), [the text] makes known the nature of the Self; likewise:
"There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).
Thus, it makes known the nature of its sovereignty;
and [it is said], "He has freedom of movement in all worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2).
Furthermore, designations such as "the omniscient one" and "the lord of all" will likewise be appropriately established in this way. // 5 //
"Auḍulomi [says] that [the Self is] by means of pure consciousness alone, because it has that as its essence (tadātmakatva).

Even though qualities such as being free from evil (apahatapāpmatva) are taught as distinct attributes, nevertheless, these are merely born of verbal conceptualization (śabdavikalpa); for in that context, only the cessation of evil and so forth is understood."
Since consciousness alone is the essential nature of this Self, it is logical that its manifestation occurs solely through that nature.

And thus, scriptural passages of this kind will be supported, such as: "Verily, my dear, this Self is without interior and without exterior, an entire mass of consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13).

As for the qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth, although they are described as attributes (*dharma*) by way of the very nature of the reality itself— as in "his desires are true"— nevertheless, because they depend upon a connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), they do not exist as part of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) like consciousness does;
for their being manifold in form has been denied.

For the multiplicity of forms belonging to Brahman has been denied in the sūtra: "The Supreme is not characterized by both [sets of] attributes even from the standpoint of its states" (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.11).

For this very reason, even the mention of laughing and so forth is intended merely to signify the absence of suffering for the sake of praise, just like the passage beginning with "delighting in the Self.
Indeed, primary forms of delight, play, and union cannot be attributed to the Self, because they necessarily involve a second object.

Therefore, the teacher Auḍulomi maintains that one becomes manifest as the self of consciousness—which is serene, indefinable, and from which the entire phenomenal world has been entirely dispelled. 6.

"Even so, on account of the mention of the prior state, Bādarāyaṇa [holds] there is no contradiction. (BBs 4.4.7) Even thus, even when the ultimate nature consisting of pure consciousness alone is admitted, there is no contradiction because, with respect to empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), the divine sovereignty of Brahman— understood from the prior [scriptural] mentions and so forth— is not denied.
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa holds this opinion. //7//
4. The Section on Volition (Saṃkalpa-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 8–9:
"But [the creation of objects] is from volition alone, because of the scriptural statement to that effect.
(BBs 4.4.8) In the Hārdavidyā, it is heard: "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers arise for him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1), and so forth.
In this regard, there arises a doubt: is volition (*saṃkalpa*) alone the cause for the manifestation of the father and others, or is it accompanied by other instrumental causes?
In this matter, even though there is the scriptural hearing that "from volition alone" [they arise], it is logical that they depend on other instrumental causes, just as in the world.

Just as in the world, for people like us, the attainment of a father and so forth occurs through volition as well as from causes such as physical movement, so it would be for the liberated one as well.
In this way, it will not be imagined as something contrary to what is seen.

However, the phrase "from mere volition" (*saṃkalpādeva*) is stated with reference to an easily available collection of auxiliary means that accomplishes the desired object, just as in the case of a king. Furthermore, fathers and others who arise from mere volition alone would not be capable of bestowing abundant enjoyment, because they would be as unstable as the manifestations of a daydream.
This being the case, we reply: "But from mere volition alone, the fathers and others arise. Why? Because of that scriptural statement:
"By his mere volition, the fathers arise" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1).
For scriptural texts such as these would be contradicted if another cause were required;
moreover, even if that other cause were to conform to one's volition (*saṃkalpa*), let it be so— but it is not accepted that there is another cause to be accomplished by a further effort,
because prior to its accomplishment, there would follow the undesirable consequence that one’s volition is barren.
Furthermore, the principle of "as in the world" (lokavat) does not apply to a matter that is to be understood through revelation (śruti).

Moreover, by the power of their resolve (saṃkalpa) alone, the stability of these [created worlds] is established for as long as required; this is because the resolve of one who is liberated is distinct from the resolve of ordinary people. // 8 //
And for this very reason, he has no other lord.
(BBs 4.4.9) And for this very reason, because his resolve is never fruitless, the wise man becomes one who has no other lord; the meaning is that he has no other master.
For even an ordinary person, when forming a resolve, does not—when another way is possible—resolve upon having someone else as his master.
And scripture shows this: "Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6).
Section on Non-existence (Abhāva-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 10–14.
Bādari says there is non-existence [of the body], for thus [scripture] declares. (BBs 4.4.10)
From such scriptural passages as, "By his mere volition, his ancestors arise" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1), it is established that the mind is the instrument of volition.
However, it is now examined whether the body and the senses exist or do not exist for the knower who has attained sovereign power.
In this regard, the teacher Bādari maintains that for the exalted knower there is an absence of both body and senses;
why?
Because the sacred tradition (Āmnāya) declares thus: "Beholding these desires with the mind, he rejoices" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.5).
"Those who are in the world of Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.13.1).
[This refers to] if, at liberation, the body and the senses [are merged] in the mind. 10.
"Jaimini [maintains] existence, because of the mention of manifoldness.
(BBs 4.4.11) But the teacher Jaimini considers that for the liberated one there is the existence of the body along with its senses, just as there is of the mind;
for it is said: "He becomes onefold, he becomes threefold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2).
By such statements, they teach the manifold conceptualization of non-existence.
Indeed, this manifold nature could not be direct without a difference in the bodies [of the liberated].
Even though this manifold conceptualization of non-existence is recited in the *bhūmavidyā* (knowledge of the earth), which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), nevertheless...

This very sovereignty, which exists even in the state of possessing qualities (saguṇa), is proclaimed for the purpose of praising the knowledge of the Infinite (bhūmavidyā); therefore, it presents itself as the fruit of the saguṇa-vidyā. // 11 //
It is said:
"Bādarāyaṇa [holds] it to be of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice.
Furthermore, the teacher Bādarāyaṇa, because he observes scriptural indications of both kinds, considers it to be rightly of both kinds: when he wills embodiedness, then he becomes embodied.
But when there is bodilessness, then [he is] "bodiless," because of the truthfulness of his volition and because of the variety of his volitions.
It is like the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*);
just as the twelve-day sacrifice is both a sacrificial session (*sattra*) and a non-session (*ahīna*), because both characteristics are seen in the scriptural texts, so too is this [case]. 12.
In the absence of a body, [the objects of desire] are possible as in the state of dream; (BBs 4.4.13).

When there is the absence of the body—that is, the physical frame together with the senses—then, just as in the intermediate state (*saṃdhyasthāna*), even though the body, the senses, and their objects do not exist, the desires for fathers and so forth consist of mere perception, so too they would be in liberation. Thus it is.
For this is logically consistent. // 13 //
In the case of existence, it is like being awake.
Furthermore, just as in the waking state the desires for fathers and so forth exist while the body is present, so too is this possible for the liberated one. (4.14)
6. The Section on the Lamp (Pradīpa-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 15–16: "The entry [of the soul] is like that of a lamp; for thus scripture shows" (BBs 4.4.15);
"Jaimini [holds this] to be a state [of the soul], because of the mention of various forms" (Brahma-sūtra 4.4.11).
Thus, in this context, the state of being embodied is stated for the liberated one.

Regarding that, when there is the creation of multiple bodies in such states as the "threefold existence" (tridhābhāva) and so forth, a doubt arises: are these bodies created without a self (*nirātmaka*), like wooden automata, or are they with a self (*sātmaka*), like our own bodies?
In that regard, because a distinction between the self and the mind is untenable, and because [the self] is conjoined with only one body, the other bodies are without a self.

This being the case, the following is established: "The entry [of the soul] is like that of a lamp. Just as a single lamp, by virtue of its power of transformation, attains the state of many lamps, so too the wise one, though being one, attains a manifold state through the possession of sovereign power (aiśvarya) and enters all bodies.
Why? Because the scripture demonstrates the manifold state of a single being: "He becomes onefold, he becomes threefold, fivefold, sevenfold, ninefold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2), and so forth.
This is not possible if one accepts the analogy of a wooden machine, nor if one accepts the entry of other living beings (jīvas).
Furthermore, the functioning of bodies devoid of a self is not possible.
As for the objection that, because a distinction between the self and the mind is untenable, the connection with multiple bodies is impossible— this is not a fault.
Because of his power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*), he will create other bodies, each endowed with a mind, following after his single mind.

And once those [bodies] have been created, the Lord's status as their presiding controller will be appropriate through the differentiation of the Self as well, due to the distinction of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
This very process is the practice of yogis in the Yoga scriptures regarding the employment of multiple bodies. 15.

But how can the sovereignty of the liberated one—characterized by such things as entering into multiple bodies—be admitted, when [the scriptures state]: "Then by what should one know whom? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15);
"But there is not a second thing existing, other than that, distinct from it, which he might know" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.30);
and "He becomes one with the water, a seer without duality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32)?

Since such scriptural passages as these preclude specific cognition, the author reads the following reply: "It refers to either deep sleep or union, for this is made manifest [in scripture]. (BBs 4.4.16). "Deep sleep" (*svāpyaya*) means *suṣuptam* (the state of profound sleep), according to the scriptural passage: "He has gone to his own self; therefore they say of him, 'he sleeps' (*svapiti')" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
Perfection is absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), according to the Vedic scripture: "Being Brahman, he attains Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).
With reference to either of these two states, this statement regarding the absence of specific designations is made.

In some places it is stated with reference to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), and in others with reference to the state of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*). How is this known? Because right there, by virtue of the context, this has been made manifest: "Having arisen from these elements, one vanishes after them; there is no consciousness after death" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad), and "But where for him everything has become the Self alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "Where, being asleep, he desires no desire and sees no dream" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.19; Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 5).
However, this state, which is the ripening of knowledge with attributes (saguṇa-vidyā), is a different state like heaven and so forth, wherein this sovereignty is described.
Therefore, there is no fault. // 16 //
7. The Section on the Activity of the World (Jagadvyāpārādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 17–22:
"Excluding the activity of the world, because of the context and because of non-proximity.

(BBs 4.4.17) A doubt arises as to whether those who, through meditation upon the Brahman with attributes, attain union (*sāyujya*) with the Lord together with their very minds, possess sovereignty that is unlimited or rather limited.

What, then, is the conclusion? Their sovereignty must indeed be absolute, as it is said: "He attains self-rule" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.6.2) and "All the gods bring him tribute" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.5.3).
"Regarding them, there is freedom of movement in all worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2; 8.1.6), and so forth—based on such scriptural passages.
This being the position reached, the author of the Sūtras states: "Excluding the activity of the world."

Excluding the activity of creating the world and so forth, another form of sovereignty consisting of powers such as *aṇimā* may belong to the liberated souls; however, the activity of creating the world belongs only to the eternally established Lord. Why? Because He is the subject under discussion there, whereas for others, He is not proximate. Indeed, the Supreme Lord alone is authorized over the activity of creating the world.
This is because, with reference to that very [Self], there is instruction regarding its origination and so forth,
and because it is the basis for the term "eternal.
However, it is heard in scripture that the other powers, such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and so on, belong to those [others] only after they have first sought and desired to know that [Self].

Therefore, they are not present in the activity of the world. Furthermore, because they possess minds, if there were a lack of consensus among them—such that one intended stability while another intended destruction—conflict might occasionally arise.

If, however, it were argued that there is no conflict because the intention of one follows the intention of another, then it is established that the others are entirely dependent upon the will of the Supreme Lord. 17

If it is argued that [the knower of Brahman attains absolute sovereignty] because of a direct scriptural instruction, we say no, because that statement refers to those situated within the [divine] circles who hold specific offices.

Regarding the claim that since there is a direct instruction such as "He attains self-sovereignty" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.6.2), it is logical that the wise possess unimpeded lordship— that must be refuted.
To this it is replied: this is not a fault,
because [the statement] refers to one who resides within the maṇḍala of those holding office.
The attainment of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) is said to depend entirely upon that Supreme Lord who resides in special abodes such as the solar orb and is the presiding authority (*adhikārika*).
For this reason, the text immediately following says, "He attains the Lord of the Mind" (*āpnoti manasaspatim*, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.6.2).
What is meant is that he attains Him who is the eternally established Lord, the master of all minds.

And in accordance with that very [principle], the text immediately following states: "He becomes the lord of speech, the lord of sight, the lord of hearing, and the lord of discernment" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.6.2).
Thus, in other instances as well, one should apply the principle that the sovereignty of others is entirely dependent upon the eternally established Lord, according to what is appropriate. // 18 //
"And it does not abide in modification; for thus the scripture declares its state.

(BBs 4.4.19) Furthermore, the supreme Lord's form, which is eternally liberated, does not abide in modification alone; rather, the locus [of the soul] is not merely the sphere of modifications such as the solar orb.
For the sacred tradition declares His twofold state: "Such is His greatness, and yet the Person is even greater than that."
"One foot of Him is all beings; His three feet are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6),
and so forth.
Nor can it be said that others who have other objects of focus attain that immutable form, because they do not have that as their primary purpose.

Therefore, it should be understood that just as [devotees] fail to reach the qualityless form of the Supreme Lord when he possesses two forms and remain fixed in his qualified form alone, so too, even those with qualities fail to reach unimpeded sovereignty and remain fixed in a state of limited sovereignty. // 19 //
And thus they demonstrate perception and inference;
and Śruti and Smṛti demonstrate that the supreme light undergoes transformation and recurrence:
"The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15).
"Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.14, Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.10," and also, "Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.6).
Thus, the intention is that the quality of being the revolving center for all transformations is well-established for the supreme light. // 20 //

"And because of the mark of equality in respect to enjoyment alone" (Brahma Sūtra 4.4.21). For this reason as well, the sovereignty of those who rely on the evolutes is not absolute, since it is heard in scripture that their enjoyment alone is equal to that of the eternally established Lord: "They say of him: 'Verily, the waters are measured; that world is his,'" and "As he [the Lord]..."
"All beings protect the deity; in the same way, all beings protect one who knows this.
Therefore, he wins union with and residence in the same world as that deity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23)—from such indicative marks of the designation of difference. // 21 //

Now, if this were so, because their sovereignty is characterized by degrees of excellence, it would be finite; consequently, it would follow that these [liberated ones] must return. To this, the venerable teacher Bādarāyaṇa provides the answer:
"No return, on account of the scriptural statement; no return, on account of the scriptural statement" (Brahma Sūtra 4.4.22).

Those who, by means of the path of the gods—consisting of the stages beginning with light and accompanied by the channels and rays—reach the world of Brahman, which is described with specific attributes in the scriptures...

Having reached that world of Brahman—wherein flow the rivers Ara and Niya; where, in the third heaven from here, stands the Aśvattha tree called Somasavana; wherein lies the invincible city of Brahmā; and wherein is the golden palace built by the Lord, which is elaborately described in various places such as the Mantras and Arthavādas—they do not return after having attained it, unlike those who have experienced their enjoyments in the world of the moon and other such realms.

Why? Because of the scriptural statements: "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6; Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.16), and "For them there is no return" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15).
This is known from such scriptural statements as, "He attains the world of Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1), and "And he does not return again" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1).

Furthermore, even though sovereignty is finite, the manner in which there is no return has been described in the passage: "At the dissolution of the effect, [the soul goes] from here with its presider to what is beyond" (Brahma-sūtra 4.3.10).

However, for those whose darkness has been utterly destroyed by perfect knowledge (*samyag-darśana*) and who are intent upon eternally established liberation, non-return is indeed already accomplished;
for it is precisely by taking refuge in that [knowledge] that non-return is established for those intent upon eternally established liberation.
For in this way, the non-return [to saṃsāra] is established even for those who take refuge in the qualified [Brahman].
"Non-return, from the word; non-return, from the word"—this repetition of the sūtra indicates the completion of the treatise. // 22 //

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpāda, the supreme wandering ascetic teacher.
This Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Brahma-sūtras is completed.
